SEASON or FARROWING.—Sows can be made to pro- duce, if desired, two litters each year. Most breeders, however, have been wisely satisfied and thankful to get one good litter. There are, of course, some exceptions, and where the breeder seeks to get the two litters, it is desirable that the dates of farrowing be so arranged that the second farrowing may come early, not later than September. MODES OF EATING GRASS.—The horse grasps the blades of grass, and then by a jerk of the head tears away the grass, and then by a side action of ,the head cuts it off. Sheep are able toget down close to the soil, while cattle, owing to their thick upper lip, cannot get so near the roots of the plants, hence cattle should be placed upon recently laid down pastimes, in preference to sheep, who. would injure the young grass by eating it off too close to the ground. COWS FOR REARING CALVES.—A COW" that is trouble-, some to milk may often be put to good use by setting her to suckling successive calves, and thus fattening them for veaL One such animal, so ugly that no milker could get near her, sucklezllher own calf and afterwards four others, which altogettfer brought her owner More than fifty dollars. This was as much money, as the milk would have brought in butter or cheese, and with much less labour.—American Cultivator. EFFECTS OF Ctinuare.—Of the cereals, as regards moisture, barley requires the driest land, wheat comes next, and oats last. Oats,, indeed, flourish in a moist climate. As regards temperature, wheat is most sensi- tive to cold, barley will grow in colder climates, while oats grow in much colder regions still; thus it is that oats have becerde SO'leirgely grown.in Scotland, 'the climate of which is not nearly so ffiNnurable to the growth of wheat. Of the leguminous crops, peas and beans require a drier atmoselfai end a warmer climate than clover or rape. Of the roots, man olds require both heat and dryness; swedes withstand more mois- ture and less warmth; and potatoes a large amount of moisture, and great variations in climate.—The Science Chatham, March 24. of Agriculture. A Lsnins' PARAD/SE.—A lady 'who sympathises with the climatic woes of which something may have been inadvertently said in this department, wants the Drawer to move over to Santa Barbara, California, which is de- scribed as a restful paradise for women. It is admitted that women make a paradise, though they have not always been successful in keeping it. At Santa Barbara the conditions of life seem easy. Not much need to bother about canned fruit, for fresh fruit la4s almost the entire, year. Strawberries and cream late in the autumn, melons, grapes, figs, pears, plums abundant, luscious Hamburg grapes one and a half cents a pound; • no trouble about servants, for a Chinaman can not only do everything faithfully, but purchase more economi- cally than his mistress; sewing is almost left out of ac- count where the seasons are so nearly the same the year round that changes are unnecessary ; society is made up of most interesting and cultivated Eastern people, who have Shakspere clubs, art circles Chataqua, musical, and Kensington cliques, and everybody is not only can- did and courteous, but capable of letting everybody else alone; and a climate so gently uniform that life is re- lieved of all household anxiety, and woman has nothing to do but to bathe, ride, drive, eat fruit, and rest. Such perfection cannot be allowed. There'll be an earthquake some time to swallow it all up.—Harper's Magazine. ESTABLISHED liawaLr 50 -YEARS. White's Celebrated Moe-Main Trusses. I shall be so gla to breathe the fresh air again It has seemed adr ful long time to be in bed. You know I was taken to the Hospital last April to be treated, for Bright's Disease of the Kidneys. Well, on the 3151 of July they tapped I me, and took away 304 ounces of water. The same thing was done again cn the 18th September, and 408 ounces of water obtained. Ort the 9th October I was discharged from the Hospital as incurable. In Janu- ary this year (the 20th), was again tapped at home and 360 ounces of water taken away. The Bt. Bar- tholomew's Hospital in Lotdon refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the St. Bartholemew'a Hospital, Chatham. also refused me, as being the worst case they had seen for years, and two local doctor. gave me up as hopeless. When I came from the Hospital it took three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an object of misery and despair. After the Hospitals had refused me and doctors given me up. my wife persuaded me to try Hop Bitters, and from he commencement have improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks and can now get down- ' stairs and walk about without even a stick. With the aid • f a few more bottles of the Sitters shall be well again. The water has entirely left my body and legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wondertul medicine. I wish 1 bad tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with doctor a' billiand other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the Hospital 1 had no appetite whatever, but since .Li s. t using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but must not mind that so long as lam getting well. Am cheerful now that recovery is near, for everyone had given me up as a bad job. With best wishes to I remain, your affect onate Brother, (Sighed) William Grayson. 1, Bush Terrace, Cage Lane, Chatham, March 14.1885. To the Hop Bitters, Co.' London. ' GIVEN AND TAKEN.. Smoothing soft the nestling head Of a maiden fancy fed, Thus a grave-eyed woman said: 'Richest gifts of those we make, Dearer than the love we take, That we give for love's own sake. Well I know the heart's unrest ; Mine has been the common quest To be loved and therefore blest. , • Favours undeserved were mine; At my feet as on a shrine , Love has laid its gifts divine. Sweet the offering seemed, and yet • With their sweetness came regret, And a sense of unpaid debt. • Heart of mine unsatisfied, Was it vanity or pride That a deeper joy denied? , "Hands that ope but to receive Empty close; they only live Richly who can richly give. "Still," she sighed, with moistening eyes,. "Love is sweet in any guise; But it's best to sacrifice.

"Be who, giving, does not crave, ,zr;•11.., Likest is to Him who gave Life itself the loved to save. Love that self-forgetful gives Shows surprise of ripened sheaves, Late or soon its own receives."—J. G. WmrrzEn.

THE SEA-WALL. tot always Summer rules the isle, Though here her chosen kingdom be Against this surf-beat wall has warred A wild and angry sea. For when, in days of old, arose Fresh from the deep this wave-washed pile, Down from his throne of mountains looked The Genius of the Isle, And bade his Titans, ocean-born, These strong abutments bring from far, Against the demons of the storm To build a mighty bar. Then wrathfully the Ocean rose; His gathered waves with sullen roar, Unbroken over, leagues of space, Came thundering to the shore. Again, again, with clouds of foam, White flying banners in his wake, He smote upon the grand sea-wall He stormed but could not break. And still the fisher furls his sail And hides from breaker and from rock, When in his hours of wrath. the Sea Renews the ancient shock. For rocks are scattered in his path Like leaves in the autumnal gale, And pallid faces drift to shore Whose dumb lips tell no tale. But while the tide shall come and go, While tempests rage and sunbeams smile, Safe guarded by its giant wall Shall bloom the Mountain Isle. —F. L Mace, Harper's Magazine.

A contract was accepted from Mr. Walker, of Westminster, to get out rock for the river walls at the rate of a shilling per cubic yard. It was resolved that the engineer should submit specifica- tions for a dredger, which one member said would probably coat £20,000. The works are being pushed forward as rapidly as possible. One of these curious death announcements, issued by the sons of a small official in the Shanghai district, is here translated and reproduced : " Calamity has overtaken our illustrious completer of probation (1). Would that I and my brothers, his un- filial sons, whose sins are truly great, could have perished ourselves. Our father, in accordance with Imperial regulations a Feng-cheng-ta-fu (posthumous title), by brevet of the fifth rank, and expectant magistrate and a district recorder, after a short illness, ended his years betweea one and two o'clock in the morning of the 20th day of the second moon, in the 13th year of Tungchi cyclical year Kwei yu, while quietly reposing on his bed at his own residence. "He was born at five o'clock in the morning of the 2nd day of the 3rd moon, in the 2nd year of Taou Kwang, cyclical year len-woo. He thus enjoyed 52 years of life. Prostrated on a bed of straw and reclining on a pillow of earth (2), we, his unfilial sons, feel that our strength is inadequate to perform the mourning ceremonies in a becoming manner. We therefore earnestly pray that Your Excellencies, Sirs, Honoured Relatives, and Elders, may bestow upon us your gracious condolence, of which we are so unworthy. Looking to you for pity and assistance, and while we shall always cherish the remem- brance of your kindness, we respectfully make the an- nouncement of our father's death. "Your cards will be received on the 25th day of the 3rd moon, on the fifth seventh (3). We, the unfilial and fatherless, while shedding bloody tears and knocking our heads on the grounds! We, the grandsons, while shed- ding tears and reverentially bowing (4)." The following explanatory-notes will aid the reader to , understand the peculiar passages in the foregone an- nouncement :—(1.) The expression is familiarly used by 1 the Chinese for a deceased father. It means that the father completed his life after successfully performing the duties of a filial son, and was a worthy living repre- sentative of his ancestors. (2.) This refers to the cus- toms of the sons of deceased persons'sleeping by the side of the coffin until it is removed. They are supposed, during the season of watching, to sleep on a bed of straw, resting with their heads on the ground or bare floor. During the time the corpse remains in the house, they keep the incense burning night and day. (3.) Funeral ceremonies continue for 49 days, counting from the death of the person. Every seventh day is a grand mourning day, and the whole is called seven days. The fifth seventh is bonsequently 'the 35th day, when extra offerigs are placed before the tablet and pictUre of the deceased. (4.) This remark is used to exhibit the greater degree of sorrow on the part of the sons. In their sorrow they shed tears of blood, and knock their heads on the ground, while the grandsons only shed ordinary tears and bow their heads. It is usual to supplement the announcement with a memoir of the deceased, printed in small blue characters on white paper. This second part Of the document reads as follows : " Our deceased father was honest in all his actions, truthful in all his words, hating and avoiding evil. While still a baby he had the misfortune to lose his father.when it devolved upon his lonely mother to care for him. Scarcely ten years of age he was bereft of his mother also, and, standing quite alone, was taken into the house of a maternal uncle. This uncle, who managed his affairs badly, soon squandered our father's small patri- mony, troubling his mind little about his education. Had it not been that our father was naturally a clever boy and fond of study, he would while living with his uncle not have learned anything. In the 29th year of Taou Kwang, at the time of the great floods in Kiangnan, a great many people came to Shanghai suffering from sick- nese, hunger, and cold. To alleviate their sufferings our father contributed what he could. In the 3rd year of Hien fang, when the red bandits raised a disturbance in Shanghai, our father, then a teacher in the north side of the city (foreign settlement), used his influence with foreigners (Western men), and thereby saved a great many people m the city from misery. In the 11th year 'of Hien fung, When the Kwang-tung bandits (the Tai- ping rebels) besieged Shanghai for seven days, the Shanghai magistrates formed a committee of defence, to patrol the streets by night and by day, of which our father was a member. For these services he was recom- mended to be a District Recorder with the fifth rank by brevet, and he remained in active Government employ- ment for the next five years. Oh! how ought we to re- - member -the straightforwardness, the public spirit, and energy of our father! Although in his last years he re- lied for his and our support on the miserable pittance 'to be got from the ink-slab (earning his living by teaching anti writing scrolls), he ever practised virtue as an ex- ample to us children. Never having too much money,he would always manage to help deserving persons in dis- ft tress, even if he should have to pawn his own clothing. Bowed down with trouble and sorrow, he found it year by year more difficult to support his large family. Added to this he suffered from ringwOrm, which nothing would cure, till last year he commenced to comfolain of giddi- ness and asthma. All medical advice having failed he at last left us (died). Oh, what misery! At this time, I (the eldest son) was absent from home, and so boakt not attend to the duties devolving upon me. • But on hearing of the calamity I returned at once, full of grief and tired of life. My second brother, who in my absence filled my place, and who cried to heaven and earth to shorten his days and add them to our father's life, had not been able to prevent this calamity. Our two mothers being still alive, and my brothers still young, I found it to be my duty to expose the pangs of grief I felt, and though scarcely able, I commenced to attend to the funeral rites, in order to at least redeem the Io,oooth part of my deadly sins. Prostrated on a bed of straw and reclining on a pillow of earth, I am too overcome with grief to say more. The unfilial son, kneeling and shedding bloody tears." , The reference to "our two mothers," in the above document, directs attention to a singular domestic arrangement existing among the Chinese. In: China, the position of the wife is honourable and important, while that of the concubine is inferior and of little esteem in a family. But the concubine was the wife's sister in the case under notice, and she was mentioned as a mother out of respect for the first wife. It fre- quently happens that a husband will bring a concubine into his house, and, as a means of preventing some of the evil consequences of the introduction, the wife will prevail on her own sister to become the husband's concu- bine. The bodies of deceased persons are not unfrequently kept in the house for years' and this invariably occurs when the family is too poor to pay for the proper per- formance of th, funeral rites. On the death of a father, the members of a family at once clothe themselves in white garments, and they gather round the corpse, sitting on the floor, weeping and crying loudly. Women are hired at such times, as mourners, who join in the lamentations, and they exhibit the most frantic signs of Fief. But the weeping is mostly feigned; at all eitents it is so on the part of 'he females, whose wailing is per- fectly ear-splitting. The duty of baying water for the purpose of washing the corpse devolves upon the eldest son, or the nearest male descendant, and it is also cus tomary for him to narne the persons who shall wash the remains. The water is obtained from the nearest stream or fountain, and on the way thither it is customary for persons composing the party to cry and groan in the most outrageous manner. The son fills the bowl with water, leaving some cash near the spot to signify that it is paid for, when the weeping is stopped, and he and his:friends quietly return to the house. After the washing of the body, the attendants dress it in many suits of best clothing, such as the deceased wore during life, and a hat is placed on his head and Silk shoes on his feet. This dressing Of the remains is a very neces- sary part of the ceremony, as it is supposed to enable the deceased to appear well dressed in the presence of his ancestors and those superiors who have preceded him into the land of spirits. When the dressing is complete, and the body quite ready for the coffin, it is usual -for some one to put gold or silver coins in the dead man's mouth ; these are supposed to be used by the spirit in paying its way into the next world. Afterwards the priests assemble to perform the funeral rites, bringing with their sacred books the drums and flutes, without which •no ceremony in China would be complete. They sit at the feet of the corpse, with a kind of altar-stone before them, around which they arrange lighted candles and burn incense sticks. When the priests sing the funeral song—always in a shrill, monotonous tone—they are accompanied by the lamentations of the family, and the howling of the hired mourners, who recite the good actions performed by the deceased and his excellencies as a filial son. During the interval, also, members of the family burn different articles of wearing apparel near the feet of the deceased, believing that the smoke will afterwards change int() garments for use in the place destined for the habitation of the soul. When the position of the family will not allow orthe burning of silk or cotton garments, they resort to paper substitutes, and maintain that the spirits are content with the sacrifice. On the second day it is usual to place the remains in the coffin, the priests taking part in the ceremony, chanting their songs the mean- while. The coffin is large and heavy, constructed of planking four or five inches thick, and is lined with cement. The body is laid on a bed of paper, with wedges fitted on each side to keep it in place; when the cover is fastened down it is hermetically sealed and rendered perfectly air-tight. It is no unusual thing for people, to have their coffins by them for many years, and when parents have completed their sixty-first year it is a very suitable birthday gift from their children! After the completion of the ceremonies the coffin is carried into a room on the ground floor and rested over two benches; the,foot of the coffin is always placed in the direction of the principal door of the house. Food and fruits are spread on a table in the rootn„an oil lamp burning all the time ; aid there the body remains until the day of burial. The lighted lamp is to enable the spirit of the dead man to find the food prqvided for its refreshment The food is renewed and the lamp is trimmed every day. The minigtrations of the priests, and the wailing of the family and hired women are repeated at the end of a week; and these ceremonies are performed every seventh day until the expiration of the customary seven weeks during which the funeral rites 'continue. The family then select the place of burial. In no part of China are the dead collected in graveyards in the cities'; in the South ef China the southern slope of a hill is selected, while in the North, where the country is level, the dead are interred in the gardens and fields. It is the professional occu- pation of an individual to explore the ground and select ' the site of a grave suitable for the repose of the dead. It is most important to the Chinese having a grave on the hillside, and that the torrent should not disturb the last abode of their dead, although it is counted a lucky spot when the site is in the view of the water. The geomancers very often protract their decisions,pretending that the locality is infested with evil spirits, as a means of magnifying their own importance and increasing the reward; and it has occasionally happened that another ' death has occurred in the family while one corpse still I I remained unburied. When the site of the grave is fixed, and the ground inspected by the family, a day is ap- pointed tor the funeral, and in this ceremony the relatives I and friends are invited to take part. Dr. Williams has written an excellent description of a Chinese funeral, and we have his permission to use the paragraph. Certainly nothing could be more accurate, and very few foreign residents in China acquired a wider knowledge than he of Chinese affairs, in private and official relations. The doctor writes :—" When the day of interment arrives, the friends assemble at the house. A band of musicians accompanies the procession, in which is also carried the ancestral tablet of the deceased in a separate sedan, accompanied sometimes by a sacri- fice, and the tablets of the offices and dignities of the family. The mourners are dressed entirely in white, or wear a white fillet round the head; the sons of the de- eased must put on the expression and habiliments of woe, and the eldest is at times supported along the street to the grave in all the eloquence and attitude of grief, although it May have been years since his father went to wander among the genii.' The women (and children Of the family follow, and at intervals cry and wail. A man goes ahead and scatters paper money in the way to purchase the good will of such wandering spirits as are prowling about. Different figures and banners are car- ried according to the means and rank of the family, which, with the friends and crowd attracted by the show, sometimes swell the train to great length. The grave is deep, and lime is freely mixed with the earth thrown in. A body is never put into an old grave while anything re- mains of the former occupant. Crackers are tired, liba- tions are poured out, and prayers:recited ; and after- wards papers, folded in the shape of clothes, horses, money, and everything he can possibly want in the land of shadows, are bidned for the use of the deceased. The tablet and sacrifice are then carried back, and the family feast on the latter, or distribute it among the poor around the door, while the The Chinese are strongly wedded to these singular cere- monies; and a man who failed to celebrate the funeral rites would incur the most bitter displeasure of the re- latives and friends., Sometimes, when the family is too poor to purchase a grave, they will keep the tcoffined re- mains perhaps for years in their small dwelling, eating and sleeping and making merry until they save a sufficient amount to employ the geotnancer land buy a grave. Perhaps no men in the world so (completely ;invest the subject of death with quaint and poetic periphrases as do the Chinese. They never refer to a deceased relative or friend as being dead; some graceful euphemism is used to remove from the Wind the sense and sting of bereave- ment; and many of the phrases in current use deserve the tribute of attention. The common foe of humanity has little terror for the sons of Han; and [certainly, in Many cases, the inevitable is regarded with a seasoning of philosephy by the Chinese. A Chinaman would never say his friend was dead. "His name has been added to the muster-roll of ghosts" would be the language used to inform us of his death. "He has become a spirit" is a metaphor equally impressive. "He has become one of the ancients is a speech !strikingly poetical and sig- nificant, remembering the ancestral form of worship of the Chinese. "He has returned to. the shades," "He has taken farewell of the world," "He has gone the long journey," are expressions all very frequently used when speaking of the dead. But the Chinese are not without unfeeling phrases on the same subject. Still it is not 'customary for them to make use of such expressions when mentioning deceased friends. "He has swallowed his breath" is a quaint periphrasis; but to "slip his akin," or "stretch his legs," are objectionable and vulgar speeches. "Hp has 'mounted upon the dragon's back to be a Ghost on High "is ,the apotheosis of an emperor. "The mmintain has collapsed" refers to a dead emperor. "The dream is over" is the exquisite and truthful reference to the death of a prince. A former emperor, •ahnouncing the death of his stepmother, sent the fol- lowing communication to his Ministers :—" We have attended her Majesty since we received the throne, and have cherished her for twenty-nine years. We have seen that in her declining days she had every comfort, and that she had passed the age of eighty, for which out heart was happy and calm, and we encouraged ourself that she would happily add one year to another, until she enjoyed the felicity of geeing a century.. Lately, on the 19th day of the moon, she took an airing in the gar- den, and returned to her palace. We daily went to inquire concerning her health, and then unexpectedly became aware that Our beloved relative was not in her usual vigour. We thought that if she was nursed a few days with care, she would then recover her health. But contrary to all our anticipations, her ailments daily in- creased in violence, and on the 24th, in the middle of the afternoon, she drove the fairy chariot, and went the long journey. Our grief broke out in long lamentations, for we are greatly afflicted. We humbly brought to mind that since the Holy Empress, Filial Pure Bright' (his own mother), left this world to take the upward,lourney we have been greatly indebted to her Imperial Majesty Ta-hing, fer her abounding kindness, and overshadowing favour. We have been made happy while attending to her,behests,as men aretejoiced by the sun which pro- longs their lives; but now we can never again look upon her affectionate countenance. Our grief cannot easily be assuaged." Mourning habiliments among the Chinese are varied and complicated in character, authorised by Imperial edicts, and regulated according to the relationship of' the deceased to the wearer. The degrees of mourning are five, collectively known as the "Five Clothes." They include "Cut Sackcloth," the "Year's Clothes," the "Greater Duty," the "Lesser Duty," and the "Hempen Cloth," representing periods of three years, one year, nine months, five months, and three months. The "cut sackcloth" is made without stitches, or, at all events, no more are used than are necessary to hold the garment together. Formerly it was simply a strip of cloth folded over the breast. The sackcloth is put aside 'after one hundred days. The three years' mourning is *brn for husbands, own fathers, adoptive fathers of the same surname adopting a junior kinsman to be his heir, and fathers who for similar motives have adopted strangers. For mothers, either wives or concubines ; mother-in-law, being the wife of the man whose concu- bine is the mother of the wearer; step-mqther, being the sister of the mourner's mother, married by the father after death of first wife; adoptive mothers and wives of adoptive fathers as already named. When the death of any of the above-mentioned relatives takes place, the mourner at once removes the black silken plait from the end of his.gueue' substituting for it a white one, and re- places the black silk knot on theecrown of his cap with one of white twisted silk. *ln actual practice the period of three years' mourning expires the day after the second anniversary, or two years and one day after the death; but the white knot is worn the whole time. In addition to the period of deep mourning, there are other terms of one year, one hundred days, sixty days, and forty-nine days. The year succeeding the three of (deep mourning a yellow plait and yellow knotrare worn, the white ones being sacrificed at the altar of the deceased ancestors. During the periods of one hundred, sixty, and forty-nine I days blue plaits and blue knots are similarly substituted. ' The first class of mourning, therefore, actually extends over three years and a half; and during the five sub- terms of mourning succeeding the three years' period, no red canbe worn. Grey clothing is generally used during the sub-terms. The prescribed mourning of wives for hus- bands is even more severe, and they must never after- wards wear gay colours qf any description. It is con- sidered disgraceful for a woman to marry again, and instances have been known of severe penalties being im- posed on families for allowing it. Unless the emperor grants a special dispensation, high officials must retire from their duties during the three years of mourning, and in no case can they retain their post during the hundred days next following the death of a parentltis currently believed that the three years' period of mourn- ing represents the time a child is suckling at the b.reasth. The Athena= says that Mr. Archibald Forbes is en- gaged in preparing for immediate publication a bio- graphy of the German Emperor, with special reference to the important part he has played in the military cam- paigns wherein he has been a conspicuous personage. . Mr. W. J. Harrison, of Birmingham, has received the Darwin Medal for the encouragement of research, founded by the Midland Union of Scientific Societies in honour of Darwin, for his original researches in connec- tion with the geology of the Midland Counties.— Atheneum. 4 The movement in'favour of Russian music seems likely to increase. A concert furnished exclusively by composers of that nationality is to be given at the Ant- werp Exposition, and Solovieff's " Cordelia," a work which has not hitherto been performed, will be put on the stage of the Imperial Opera at Vienna, with Madame Pauline Lucca in the principal part, early next season. A LONG-LOST PORTRAIT of Sch i iller s said to have been discovered by Administrator Trinks, of Meiningen, in the old pilgrimage resort of Grimmenthal, near that town. It is a chalk drawing, and was taken by the well- known Meiningen painter, Reinhard, in 1789, when Schil- ler was staying with his sister at Meiningen. The face is not so meagre and long as in most of the portraits of the poet; but there "is something wonderfully fas- cinating," says the finder, "in the ideal and yeLstreich expression of the eyes and mouth."—Atheneum. A MICROSCOPIC Boox.—The Nation says that when the microscopic edition of Dante (" Dantino ") saw the light at Padua in 1878 it was thought to be the smallest book in existence. But its nose was put out of joint by the discovery at Florence, in 1881, of an " Officiolum (Venice, Mind, 1649) only 31 mm.* wide and 50 mm. high. But this had evidently been cut down in rebinding, and is therefore considered to be larger than an " Officio- lum " just discovered, also from the Giunti press, which has never been under the binder's knife, and in the brigi- nal cover measures 33 by 48 mm. Thus bibliography, like microscopy, penetrates further and further into the Liliputiaia world. [*A millimetre is rather less' than 1-25th of an inch, i.e. '03937.J ELECTRIC SIGNALLING FROII BALLOONS—An invention, , which it is anticipated will be of importance in future lwarfare, was on Monday night exhibited in the grounds iof the Albert Palace, by Mr. Eric S. Bruce, the inventer, llt consists of the application of electric lighting to balloons, by means of which signals, may be flashed at night over very wide areas. Before giving a practical demonstration of the working of his invention, Mr. Bruce delivered a brief lecture in the concert hall of the Albert Palace, in which he stated the results of his ex: periments, said explained the manner in which he had arrived at them. The invention consists of an ordinary balloon, made of a material as translucent as possible (in the case of the one at present on exhibition the material is canabric),-in which are fixed a number of incandescent lamps. The balloon is a captive one, and the rope:which secures it is also Utilised for conveying the electric cur- rent to the lamps inside the balloon. The Morse system of telegraphy is employed for the signalling, which illuminates the balloon with flashes of light of longer or shorter duration. The invention dates back only two months, an the experiments were made with a large balloon for the first time on Monday night, and were completely successful. It is proposed to continue the exhibitions of signallin,g for a month. The chief obStacle to be overcome in introducing the electric light into the balloon was that occasioned by the highly inflammable nature of the,gas with which the balloon is inflated. This has, however, been successfully surmounted. During the evening, several sentences; including A' God save the Queen, "Rule Britannia," and "Health and, happinesS to *Princess Beatrice," were flashed from the balloon. ANTI-CHOLERA VACCINATION.—III a second communica- tion which ' Dr. Ferrari has forwarded to the Paris Academy of Sciences be denies that ,he has manifested any desire td keep secret his method Of anti-cholera vac- cinations. It consists, he says, in inoculation into the cellular tissue of cultures of the "comma" bacillus of maximum virulence. The bacilli are cultivated in a very nutritive infusion, and are not "attenuated." The aeration of the cultures favours the intensity of the virulence and produces a better "vaccine." The dose employed is one cubic centimetre in each arm, and three successive inoculations are necessary to confer immu- nity, the total quantity of the " vaccine " administered being therefore six cubic centimetres. An interval of five days is allowed between each inoculation. Dr. Fer- ran declares that systems of a mild choleraic character are produced by the inoculations, and that in the locali- ties where the inoculations have been practised on a large number of persons the curve showing the rise and decline of the epidemic has been modified in the most gratifying mariner. He is unable to say how long the protective influence lasts, but it appears to be for at least two months. The morbid symptoms following the in- oculations appear to be produced, "like those of cholera," says Dr. Ferran, from a mysterious influence on the nerve centres. Dr. Ferran has formally applied for the prize of £4,000 left by M. Brebant in 1849 for award by the Academy to the discoverer of "an efficacious remedy- for cholera or "the causes of the disease." One of the specified achievements which would entitle a candi- date to receive the prize is "the discovery of a certain prophylactic as infallible, for instance, as vaccination for smallpox." M. Paul Bert expressed a hope that Dr. Fer- ran would send some tubes of the " vaccine" for ex- amination and experimentin Paris.

div.head: SHALL WE REPUDIATE FREE 'TRADE? BY R. withasm.
div.p: SHALL WE REPUDIATE FREE 'TRADE? BY R. withasm.

It has been well said that "figures may be made to prove anything." If this be so, it is all the more, es- sential for the country's welfare, that not only figures but the experience gained by comparing to- day with- forty years ago, should be called in to help in the decision. A General Election is approaching. and the Conservatives are anxious to win power, and it becomes a matter of great necessity to them to search and find out some great rallying cry. No plausible means will be left untried; no matter how foolish or suicidal it may be to the nation, the Tories calculate upon it turning over to their side a sufficient number of voters to enable them to, accomplish their object. Thus they have seized upon the catch phrase "Fair Trade " as the one thins to suit their par. pose. "Why do Free Traders object to Fair Trade ?" they ask ; "Surely there is nothing wrong in it." We answer them plainly, "We do not object to Fair Trade ;" we invite it as a principle dear to our poli- tical treed, and endeavour by all means in our power to persuade other nations to accept it, but you cannot rut old heads upon youngshoulders. Experienee has to be bought we concluded the purchase forty years ago. Other natioas younger than ourselves in the ways of commerce are, according to the newspapers, learning in the school of affliction. Why do you object to commissions of inquiry also? they ask. Our answer is plain—because they produce so little good. In 1879 a commission was appointed by the Beaconsfield Government. It cost the nation no,ooo or Leo,ooo, yet what good has it done? The ink is scarcely dry, are we have another committal= appointed Whose labours will extend over a series of years;, a report will be issued, and there the whole thing will end. It is possible for men to become so wedded to one idea that to remove it would require a surgical opera- tion. Such a one we have in Warrington. Writing sometimes as T. Lawreason, at others as a "Well- known Writer," thie gentleman looks to Proteetion to make up for the skill he may lack in the trade in which he is engaged, and is now employing his time in abusing the only capable minister the Tories ever had—Sir Robert Peel. In looking around for the cause of our depression in trade, I am afraid our Fair Trade friends persist in seeing the mote in our neigh- bour's eye, while ignoring the beam that troubles their own visual organs. ' The causes of bad trade are many. It has been at- tempted to be proved that at stated and foreseen in- tervals, a period of bad trade must, in the ordinary course of nature's laws, come about, and consequently we have no right to grumble. If it were possible to give this mathematieal proof, steps might be taken to at least , make _preparation for each succeeding calamity. This theory not being accepted, we must look further afield, It is no contradiction in terms to say, that although we are suffering for want of trade, yet Warrington it to-day in the positiog of having a greater output than' ske ever had before; and it is possible that this increa&d production, coupled with, the large amount of capital .attracted .for manufactur- ing purposes, has something to do with our depres- sion.

Throughout manufacturing Europe a system pre- vails that happily we, in this tight little island, have got rid of—that is working ,long and unreasonable hours, and employing children and women at all trades and all hours; for this we shall in a measure suffer. nonesty in trade has become a by-word, as any one may see who studies the trade columns of the newspapers. It is hard .for manufacturers to resist temptation—and adulteration goes hand in hand with low wages—in the eager desire to outstrip other coun- tries. To imitate articles in great demand is the chief aim. In India and China the inhabitants use large quantities of cotton cloths, and to stiOcessfully com- pete in supplying these Lancashire mill-owners have freely used China clay. The Times of July 26, 1876, reported "that as much as 80 per cent. of adulteration was possible. and • was not unfrequently practicable. In 18.73 a remotittrance against this disreputable practice was sent to the Manchester Chamber of Com- room, from that of Shanghai ; but the Manchester Chamber " after a long discussion decided that,lt would be wise not to interfere with the present prac- tices." Mr. Byrne in his book, "Outlines of an In- dustrial Science," quotes ,from the Times of India which says*-" The local mill industry owes its MA: [• oafs mainly to the dissatisfaction of the purchasers of . Manchester goo& with the dishonest system of mix- ing with the cotton some 30 per cent. of China clay." The same writer gives instances where a duty of 10 per cent, was imposed by the local legislature of Mel- bourne with the view ,of keeping Yorkshire shoddy out of the market, because it was made to imitate the . genuine article. "

The silver question is one, and not the least of our troubles in pushins trade with India. Th,e National Review of Novell-04er, 1884, contains, a )3orrespondence from Wong Plfts, Commissary General of the Bombay Army, which will well repay our Fair Trade friends all the trouble of perusal. He says in effect, "We make the natives of India change all their money into gold before we will trade with them." What is the effect? In, Bombay "scores of mills have been built for making cotton cloths, and •the rate of exchange Is stimulating this industry." And he says "the stimulus of dear gold will, sooner or later, lead to the building of mills for the weaving of bioad clothe Fair Traders want a Oemmitision of Inquiry to learn these things; here they are ready to their hands. The Colonel goes on to say that Indian officials have lists of imported articles givin, into their hands, and are told, " to purchase oflndian manufactures, the loss by exchange in purchasing them of English make being prohibi- tive." Tho very able writer concludes by saying, "The trade of England, instead of competing for the £1,400,000,000 or 1,500,000,000 of gold and silver bullion available to it, is scrambling for a share of the £700,000,000 of gold available.'

Sir Jules Vogel, Cdlonial Treasurer of New Zealatid, speaking of our trade with that colony says, "There has been a great deal of scamped work and adulteration going 9n, and that it is only by a happy accident—an iron axle falling to the ground and ' breaking while being unshipped—that we were saved from sending forth death and destruction on our rail- ways by using rotten axles sent out from Great Britain." We see from this, one cause of our bad trade is that it is carried on on the "cheap and nasty" principle, and that our system of exchange wants altering; no need for a Commission to tell us what we already know. In your next issue, the question as affected by a want of Technical Education and a more liberal system of railway charges will be dealt with.

A man nam'ed Pelsall, on Saturdav, fell down a pit 50 fathoms deep, near Coatbridge, Glasgow. His body, when recovered, was frightfully mangled. At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Wednesday, Michael O'Donnell, who was indicted for the wilful mur- der of his wife, was found guilty of manslaughter, and sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude. At a convention of Nitionalist delegates of the county of Wexford. held at Wexford on Wednesday, it was resolved to contribute £6OO to pay two parliamentary representa- tives for the county and an equal sum to the National Fund for the paymept of members of poorer consti- tuencies. °RE CASE Of Army and Navy MEDICINES contains suffi- cient to cure contagious diseases of a certain class (internal or external); 4s. 6d., parcels post ss. STATEMENT BY THE WAR SECRETARY. On a vote of £2,227,800 for war and other stores, including the minu- factuling departments, Mr. W. 11. SMITH male a state- ment with regard to the progress in naval and land service armaments, and for submarine mines. The total expendi- tor. for naval guns and proj.ctiles under the normal vote was £668,0010 ; torpedoes, £77,800 ; miscellaneous, £814,000. Out of the vote of credit the expenditure for naval guns and brojectiles was £450,000, torpedoes, £67,000; miscellaneous services, £50000; making a total out of the estimates for the year and the vote of credit together of £1,417,000 for ?I‘val armaments. With respect to land armaments, it was prorkm-d to complete the more important coaling stations before deoing with the minor ones. Works had been commenced at Hong Kong, Jimaica, Simon's Bay, Singapore, and Trincontate,.. Every effort would be made to complete the whole of the fortifications by March 31st, 1888, and in the meantime some temporary addition had been made to the armaments at certaM stations. With regard to submarke mines, it had been decided to formmni division of a Coast Corps of Royal
Engineers for instructional purposes in relation to submarine mine defences of our commercial ports—(hear,

hear)—and to form in connection with that boas, volunteer , submarine mining companies. A submatine defence organ- isation had been approved for the military ports abroad. , He proposed to nominate in conjunction with the First Lord of the Admiralty, an officer or officers to pre- pare a working scheme for each of our commercial ports, by which each of the several elements of defence should be brought into harmonious cooperation and made capable of immediate application to any sudden emergency. The navy and coaling stations would require £2.345,000 in three years. the estimate for armaments and works for military ports was £2.230 000, and for commercial ports £1.770,000, making a total of £6,425,000. Of this sum £9OO 000 had been met out of the estimates of this year and out of the vote of credit, leaving £5,525,000 to be provided in the army estimates of the next four or five years, unless it pleased Parliament and the country to hasten the completion of the work. In addition somewhat more than a quarter of a million would be needed to complete the reserve of stores. The late Government had provided £220,000 in the ordinary estimates, and to increase that supply they provided £2BO 000 in the vote of credit. It would remain to provide £270,000 in excess of the ordinary estimates of next year, altogether irrespective of any expenditure for the new small arm which had been under consideration, but without any decision being taken. He hoped the proposals would be accepted as a necessary step towards making the arrange- ments r-quired for the safety of the country. (Hear, hear.)—Discussion followed in the course of which Mr. BRAND said he statement of the Secretary for War practi• cally embraced the programme of the late Government. He regarded it as of national importance to defend the Tyne, the Clyde, and the Mersey —The vote was agreed to.—A further vote of £843,800 for works, buildings, and repairs was also agreed to. MISCELLANECRTS.—On the vote for miscellaneous effec- tive services there was a short conversation on the Conta- gious Diseases Acts, Mr. PULESTON and Mr. C. BENTINCIC complaining of their suspension and the misrepresentation I be which it had been brought about.—The vote was passed, as was also several other votes of estimates, and progress was reported. MR. BRIGHT AND MR. CALL AN. A QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.

Mr. CALLAN requested permission to call the attention of the House to a speech delivered by Mr. Bright at the dinner to Lord Spencer on Friday last. In that speech the right hon. gentleman had asked by whom charges which he described as heinous had been brought against Lord Spen- cer, and he had replied to his own question by saying that they were the Irish members whom he stigmatised as dis- loyal to the Crown. to other words he accused Irish mem- bers who had taken the oath of allegiance of being perjurers That charge he (Mr. Callan) repudiated with scorn and con- tempt. The right hon. gentleman then went on to charge the Irish members with obstruction and with sympathising with crime and criminals. Now he (Mr. Callan) contended that the Irish members had made no charges against Irish officials or judges or peers which they had not proved. The hon. member then proceeded to refer to precedents for cen- suring the right hon. member for Birmingham for a breach of the privileges of the House, to a debate on the 23rd February, 1838, when Mr. O'Connell was censured for saying that Ireland was "not safe from the perjury of English and Scotch gentry who took oaths to act according to justice and then acted according to party." He also referred to a debate which took place on the 31st March, 1873, when the Right Hon. Mr. Justice Lopes was required to apologise for having (as appeared from aa article in the Pall Mall Gazette) accused the Liberal party with allying themselves with ," a disreputable Irish band, whose watchword was Repeal of the Union." In the course of the debate Mr. Dis- raeli strongly expressed his sense of the just cause which the Irish members had to complain, and had urged the hon. member to withdraw and express regret for the language he had used. He hoped that course would be followed now by the member for Birmingham. But looking at the course he had taken on a previous occasion, he was afraid that it would not. He (Mr. Callan) denied that he had ever sympathised either with crime or criminals, and with regard to Lord Spencer, he bad never said a word against him until the murder, he might say, of Miles Joyce. (Cheers from the Irish members, and cries of indignation from other parts of the House.) The bon. member con- cluded by handing in a report of Mr. Bright's speech, and this having been read by the clerk at the table, Mr. Callan moved, in the usual form, "That the accusations which it brought against members of the House constituted a breach of privilege." Mr. BRIGHT, who was warmly cheered on risicg. com- menced by disclaiming any intention to include Mr. Callan among those members of whom he spoke on the occasion referred to. The hon. member, he presumed, came forward yesterday as the protector of his countrymen, and what he had said should have that consideration it would receive in the country after this discussion. What was the object of the banquet at which this terrible speech was made ? It was to bring together a large muster of members of both Houses of Parliament for the purpose of showing the high esteem in which they held the late Viceroy of Ireland, and for the purpose of meeting some of the charges made against him. Lord Spencer in his speech referred to many of these charges, and gave answers which certainly were satisfactory to the 200 or more gentlemen there assembled. It was natural, in considering these charges, to refer to those who made them, and to what these charges were, and into that he in his speech went a little deeper than those who had preceded him. What were the charges against Lord Spencer? The House had heard what the hon. mem- ber had just said. It shocked him, and had he heard that speech before he should have been oh leant to include the hon. member in the charges he made. it had been stated by Irish members and writers in the Irish press over and over again that Lord Spencer sent to the gallows men whom he knew to be innocent. Was ' It possible to put into words a more heinous charge? (Hear, hear.) The most guilty murderer who went to the gallows was not, if that were true, more guilty than Lord Spencer. (Hear, hear.) Would it be wrong to say that persons who brought such charges against the representa- tives of the Queen were disloyal ? He should, for himself, say that no man who made such charges was otherwise than disloyal to the Viceroy and the Crown. (Cheers.) Two years. ago Sir S. Northcote brought before the House a speech he (Mr. Bright) made at Birtnimehain in which he spoke of a Tory alliance with a re,,el party. Did Irish mem- bers repudiate the term 2 No, on the contrary, they accepted it. (Cheers). He did not believe the bon, member for Longford would accept it (Mr. Justin McCarthy made no response.) But if hon. gentlemen who sat near him were to be taken by their own words and writings some of them have a fair title to the name of rebels—(ironical cheers from the Home Rule party and loud and general cheers from the House.) Hon. gentlemen to whom he was referring had censtantly described the House of Commons as a foreign as- sembly, and referred to the late Government as a foreign administration. (Derisive cheers) • Those cheers justified his words. Only a short time ago Mr. Devitt was urged to cams to the House by a constituency ready to re- turn him. Mr. Devitt, except perhaps when 3 landlord was in question, appeared to be an honest min, and Mr. Devitt said he could not come to the House, because he could not tat:, the oath of allegiance. There were men highly respectable, honest men in Ireland, who would I make admirable members, but that would not tike the oath of allegiance -penalise they were not loyal to the Crown. These were the charges he made, and these charges were not repudiated. (Cbeere.) Then he referred to the obstruction of legislation in 1881 and 1882. The legislation he was not about to defend, but the obtruction was a fact. The only time they allowed a clause to pass was when, be withdraw- ing, they placed the Government in a minority, to ensure the insertion of a clause which they thought would make the Bill more hateful to their country than it was. He eccnsed them of assailing judges, juries, and law officers. Well, it had been said by members that Lord Spencer knowingly hanged innocent men. (Hear, hear, from Mr. Biggar.) They assailed judges, stating them tq be partisan% They assailed law officers, accusing them of packing juries', and pecked juries were necessarily corrupt. (Hear, hear.) All their utterances had been in one line of sympathy with criminals, nor had he ever heard or read of any emphatic declaration by the Irish members against criminals except

The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHESSUER said he could not but regret that Mr. Bright had not at the banquet imitated the excellent example set by the Marquis of Hartington and Lord Spencer in the moderation of the observations they made. He thought if the remarks complained of had been made in that House the right hon. gentleman would have been called to order ; but the question was not whether the language consiituted a breach of the privileges of the House, but whether they were well advised in taking notice of such language as a breach of privilege. He thought it unwise on the eve of a very hot electioe, campaign for the House to set a precedent of interfering with remarks or writings which might be proclaimed out of doors against a political party, ana there• fore, irrespective of the language which had been ueed, he was unable to support the motion.—The Marquis of HARTINOTON held that Mr. Bright had done all that the House could expect from any one of its members. He would ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer if he thought it right that no notice should be taken of those who per- sistently brought such hideous charges against Lord Spen- cer? Was it conducive to peace, order, and good govern- ment that no notice should he taken of these men? He had come to the conclusion that there was nothing in the re- marks of his right bon. friend at the benquet that was in- capable of proof, therefore he stood be him and declared the opportuneness and the justice of his remarks. Such a motion as that brought forwardewould impose a mischiev- ous restriction on liberty of speech, and be could not suppose it bad been brought forward with the general assent of the memeeers of the Irish party, he could not believe that the men who had habitually allowed themselves such license of speech as many of them had indulged in would be the men to come whining to the House to complain when one of the greatest orators in the House expressed to the people in language the trutb:of wbich was admitted by nine-tenths of the people of this country the opinions he held of the conduct pursued by certain members of the House.—Mr. T. CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT BILL.—On the motion to E 0 into Committee on the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, the HOME SECRETARY stated that it was intended to go on with it from day to day until it was closed, remarking that he did not know what arguments those who were opposing the motion would bring forward, but they would have to answer to their constituencies for their action, as there was nothing the people of this country were more determined to main- tain than the purity of their households.—Mr. HOPWOOD moved an amendment in favour of further inquiry and more deliberation before proceeding with the committee. He did not know why the Home Secretary should have in- terposed between kiln and the House, unless it was for the unbecoming purpose of making an attack on those who like himself were as much actuated by a sense of duty as the right hon. gentleman in the face of the storm upon the top of which the right hon. gentleman was now riding, though he had acquiesced all these years in the present state of things, and had even resisted the raising of the age of protection. SOLITE AFRICA.—On the vote for South Africa Colonel STANLEY said he was not able to offer any very definite in- formation as to the immediate future, but he thought the special fault of oar South African legislation in times past I had been that the hot fit of sending out expeditions had inevitably been succeeded by a cold fit of retrenchment and of leaving the colony to its own devices. In the course of a few months he hoped, taking the situation as he found it, to make the best he could of it by endeavouring to promote the welfare of the people placed under us. An offer had been made of the cession of a rather indefinite territory to the north of our protectorate, and upon that subject it would be expedient for the Government to act I with extreme care. They had already learned a lesson of the extreme danger of these vague extensions of territory, and it was by no means clear that the offer was one which the Government should accept without the greatest consideration of the future conse- quences. As the special object of Sir C. Warren's expedi- tion had been accomplished they looked forward to the early diminution of his force and to the substitution of a body of police suited to the active work which would have to be done. It was hoped that some of those engaged in the expedition might be induced to form part of the new force, the command of which had been given to Colonel Carrington.—On the motion for adjournment an appeal was made to the Government to take the Criminal Law Arnold- meat Bill as early as possible, as there was a general feel- ing throughout the country that it ought to be gone on with at ooce.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER thought it might be possible if business was proceeded with 11 rapidly to get the bill into Committee en Thursday. . _

The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. tirrup, the president of the society, and he was supported by Faieer Hall (Woolton), Fathers Brown, Fishwick, and Thompson (Weeriegton), Qaarter-Master McGarty, Messrs. Cavanagh, Cook, beeess, W. Stirrup, W. Johnson, and H. Eccles (Secretary). The dinner was served up in the host's best style, and was both as to quality and waiting everything that could be desired. This society is, it may be mentioned, in a very healthy con- dition, its funds in:band amounting to over £5OO. After dinner Tbe Rev. Father Betoever preposed the toast, "The Pope." The first and he thought the greatest toast of the evening was that of their holy father Pope Leo XIII. (Applause.) As Catholics, no matter of what nationality they might be, they all regarded the Pope as their common father; both priests and laymen looked to him as the common father of the faithful. Therefore he was sure when he proposed that health their sentiments would agree with his in every re- spect, and they wished long life and success to the Pope in his government of the church. (Hear, hear.) This was a difficult task. He had, as the scriptures said, the care of all the churches en his shoulders, and tbey knew he would be helped in his difficult duties by knowing that he pos- sessed the love and confidence of the whole Catholic body throughout the world. (Applause.) He (Father Brown) ' hat had the pleasure of meeting a friend of his who had just returned from Rome, and this person told him that in spite of all the difficulties of his position the holy father was in a very fair state of health, and better in fact than he had been for some time, 'and that the reports which appeared in many of the papers had not the slighest foun- dation in fact. (Applause). The toast was then cordially honoured. The CHAIRMAN in proposing "The Queen and the Royal Family," said it was his firm opinion that the Queen had no more loyal subjects than those who were assembled in that room. (Hear, hear.) If they looked into the history of the country they would find that whenever the mon- archy was engaged in foreign or civil war the Catholic people were always found supporting the throne, and that even when the Catholics were suffering wrong and persecu- tion at the hands of the sovereign. He believed that if at any time difficulties should again arise, if there should be either rebellion at home or war abroad, they would find the Catholics in their old places supporting loyally the king or queen. And with regard to their present Queen, he thought if all their rulers had done as little harm and as much good they would have done very well. (Hear, hear.) He thought that at the present time they might congratulate her Majesty on getting all her children happily married, at least they hoped they were happily married. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He thought they as Catholics owed a very deep debt of grati- tude to their bishops and clergy in England when they considered that not many years ago they could not assemble together as they bad done that night. As Catholics they were now uplifting their heads, and they had to thank their bishops and clergy for the perseverance they had shown and the hardships they had undergone to keep the faith alive. In speaking for himself he must say, and he said it most sincerely, that he had never met any persons who treated him kinder than the friends of War- rington. (Hear, hear.) And foremost amongst those friends were the members of the different societies in the town—of that society, and of the Temperance League, and of the emo- tion. (Applause.) The Rev. He also referred to the Catholic bazaar which is about to be held, and be asked those present and their friends to do their utmost to make it a success. Mr. P. Mather next sang "Hearts and Homes." The Secretary (Mr. Eccles), the Vice-President (Mr. W. Johnson), and the Treasurer (Mr. T. Mr. DISKIN appropriately proposed the toast of "The In- vited Guests." Mr. LYNESS, in responding, said it had been one of the greatest pleasures he had had since be cam, to Warrington to receive an invitation te that dinner. He thought that if the Catholic people of Warrington were a little more closely connected together by societies of that kind they would by and bye be not only able to keep their own, but to keep ahead of any other denomination in the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitehead having lungs humorous song, Mr. W. STIRRUP proposed "The Society." He said he was proud of that Catholic club, which gave them as much benefit, and more according to what they paid, than any other sick society in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) They were a Catholic society; they had prayers for the dead and other things which as Catholics they ought to have. It was a grand society, and it was a pity that instead of about 60 or 70 members they had not 701. (Hear, hear.) He understood that there was a Catholic society in Warrineton in 1790, and from that time they had had one; and there was a time about 20 years back when they had the finest flag in the town—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and he hoped before long that they should have another as good. (Hear, hear.) He referred to the number of Catho.ic members in the lodges of Shepherds, Druids, and Oddfellows in the town, and expressed regret that more of them did not first join that society. He thought it was the duty of every Catholic to send their children first to the Catholic club, and if that were done they would have many hundreds of memb3rs. ' (Hear, hear.) They had a good society, and monetarily theyewere prospering, and he believed that ultimately the good of the society would be seen. He was glad to see so many of their clergy present, as he did not remember having seen so many as four present before. (Applause.) Mr. ECCLES responded, and was happy to say the society was now in a prosperous condition. They would perceive from the balance mbeet that the society's funds on the 30th June amounted to £520 43 51, and if anyone would take the trouble to divide that they would find that it gave a little more than a a member. He had been reading an account of the society of the United Catholic Brethren, a society something like the Oddfellows, Druids, and Shepherds, which had twenty halls, the name which was used in- stead of lodges. He did not think twenty halls were suffi- cient for a Catholic society, while the Oddfellows numbered their thousands. The total number of its members was 1,567, and its funds amounted to £113.434, which meant about £526 14e for each hall, so that he thought that so- ciety was pecuniarily in a good position. But still it was not in so good a position as their own society, as thee had £524 4s scl for 63 members, while the other society had £521 odd for each 7S members. (Hear, hear.) He Was only sorry that. as Mr. Stirrup said, so many of the Catholic young men of Warrington instead of joining that society joined other societies. Those other societies were no doubt good societies, but when they took into consideratios that those societies paid only a similar sum to what thee did, while their contributions were higher, he ventured to think that none of them supplied the same benefits that they did. (Applause.) Mr. ECCLES also proposed the toast of " The Honorary Members," which was respotided to by Mr. Cavanagh. Mr. Cummitrford sang a humourous song, " Father O'Flynn," after which Mr. ECCLES proposed the health of the President, which was suitably responded to by Mr. A. STIRRUP. In proposing the toast of "The Medical Officer," Mr. P

Mr. WHITEHEAD also spoke in complimentary terms of Dr. Ga wy, and said that he was one of the finest officers they had had in connecion with the association. , Mr. W. STlnnvP proposed "The Town and Trade of War- rington." He said Warrington was one of the oldest towna in England, and in former days lette-s addressed to Liver- pool were marked " Liverpool, near Warrington "—(laugh- ter)—and the thought struck him that before many months were over the same thing might occur again. (Lang'ater.) He believed that when they got the ship canal Warrington ',mid flourish more than any other portion of Lancashire. (Hear, hoar.) He thought that the Corporation instead of giving £1,000.t0 the ship canal ought to have pawned the town and given 4.1.00,000. (Laughter.) Trade in Warring- ton was at present very bad, as in fact it was throughout the world. and Warrington had been one of the'last places to feel it. History told them that Warrington used to supply half the sails of her Majesty's fleet, but that trade had left the town, and file-cutting used to be one of the best trades of the town, but now it was one of the least. But they were determined to have the canal to Warrington, and if the mak- ing of it involved the taking iu of Birkenhead and Liver- pool they would do it. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) In the course of the evening other toasts and songs wero given, and altogether the dinner passed off enjoyably.
FRANCE.-MADAGASCAR.

j Pants, StaraDev.—ln the Chamber of Deputies to-day ' the new credit to defray the expenses of the French expedi- tion in M,dagascar was discussed. M. Perin strongly con- demned the policy which had been pursued with regard to ' Madagascar. Afrer a speech from M. Penal°, the debate was adjourned until Monday. PARIS, MONDAY.—The kelf Chinese Minister to France was received in audience by President Grey,' to-day, when a cordial interchange of good wishes took place. President Gr6vy, in his reply, said France could not but rejoice with China at the restoration of the former friendly relations be- tween the two Powers. At the sitting of the Chamber of Deputies, the debate of the Madagascar Credit was resumed by M. de Freycinet. who spoke at some length in defence of the policy of the Government. GREAT FIRE IN PARIS.

PARIS, SATURDAY —A fire broke OUI-larit sight in the Barienolles quarter of the city, amongst the carpenters' workshops and vast warehouses in the neighbourhood, where carpets are stored during the summer months. Five blocks of buildings containing workmen's lodgines were burnt out. The damage is enormous. It is estimated that several mil- lion franca' worth of carpets were destroyed. Several fire- men were injured, and it:is feared that there are other vic- tims amongst the reins.

div.head: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT WARRINGTON.

After a week's training the members of the Ninth Lan- cashire Rifle Volunteer Corps, Warrington and Newton, were on Saturday inspected by Colonel Thackwell, the officer in command of the Bth and 40th Regimental Dis- tricts. The weather was gloriously fine, but hot. Shortly after four o'clock in the afternoon they mustered at the Drill Hall. and soon afterwards "fell in " on the green in front of the Town Hall. Here they were formed in march- ing order, and, the word of command being given, the regimental band struck:up a stirring tune. With mien erect, regular and steady, the Volunteers marched out of the town and over a rather rough road to the drill field in Arpley Meadows, where followed a large number of people attracted by the spectacle. Arrived at the field the men, in preparation of the hard work to follow, squatted leisurely on the grass to await the arrival of the inspecting officer, who was to pat them through their facings. Those who had come to watch took advantage of a pleasant hillock at one side of the field, that nearest the river, and seated them- selves in picturesque disorder, also to await the coming of the inspecting officer and the evolutions to follow. Not until nearly half-past six did Colonel Thackwell, who was accompanied by Miss Thackwell and Captain Mansell, arrive on the field, and then commenced without further delay the earnest work of the day. 'I he men were drawn up in column, and, in their gay uniforms, though their numbers were not very great, presented a somewhat impos- ing sight. The steel of their weapons glittered in the sun- light like polished mirrors, and in the march past that fol- lowed, in column, quarter column, and double time, they drilled in a way that did credit to the Volunteer movement. Other manceuvres were gone through, strange to those ignorant of military tactics, but none the less interesting, and Majors Litton and Bolton, and Captains Ridgway and Widdows, were in turn called upon to take command, which was afterwards assumed for the rest of the evening by Colonel Greenall, who put his men through various battalion movements,'ending with the attack. This latter drill was done very creditably, and evoked the admiration of those who witnessed the proceedings. After a thorough in- spection the corps was drawn up in a compact body, and Colonel Thackwell, who was nobly mounted, addressed a few congratulatory words to the non-commissioned officers and men. They were, he said, a fine body of men, of good physique, and of smart appearance. For the silence ob- served in the ranks they were deserving of the greatest praise, and the march past had been highly satisfactory. He expressed himself as pleased with the way in which the manceuvres had been gone through, and remarked that the corps was a credit to Warrington. The Colonel then, after a few words addreesed in private to the Volunteer officers, rode off the field, and Colonel Greene!' made a short soldier-like speech to his men, who listened with attention. They had had some very hard movements to go through. and he hoped they had done them successfully. He was very much gratified with the remark their inspecting colonel made about their good appearance and physique. Their week of training had been a very pleasant one, and he had not had to mark any one in the "black book." Ttaere were several officers who had been promoted since they last met, and one officer on the ground —Quartermaster Hatchinson—looked remarkably well in .his new uniform. Quartermaster Hutchinson was one of their oldest volunteers, and one whom be delighted to see in officer's uniform. Major Litton, Major Bolton, Captain Buckton, and he himself, had also received promotion. After promotion it was usual to drink to the health of those who received the honour, and that custom would not in the present instance be departed from. Colonel Greenall then made a short explanation with reference to a misunder- standing about 2s each being paid to the men instead of their having the usual dinner, an arrangement which, he said, though it was no doubt made with the best intentiens, he could not fall in with. He and the other officers had agreed that on the whole it was better to adhere to the old custom of roast beef and plum pudding, as, if the principle of payment for services was introduced it would in itself be fatal to the volunteer movement. Volunteers were to a certaia extent soldiers, and it was not for a soldier to ques- tion a command—" His not to reason why, his but to do and die." He should always consider every individual, and try to meet and conciliate any member who had a grievance, but he should always command their support in endeavouring to lay down such rules as he believed to be best for the corps. The colonel was frequently applauded clurisg this address. Oa its conclusion the corps again for- med in marching order and proceeded to the Drill Hall by way of Wilson Patten-street, Bridge-street, and Sankey- street. At headquarters a repast had been prepared under the superintendence of Mr. O'Brien, to whiei the sharpened appetites of the volunteers did full justice. The total num- ber present at the inspection was 549, which included 13 officers, 34 sergeants, 50 bandsmen and buglers. and 441 rank and tile, with ohe sergeant and Sour rank and file at- tached by authority. One officer, two sergeants, and 16 rank and file were absent with permission, and six privates without. The officers present were Colonel Greenall, Major and Ad jut int O'Leary, Majors Litton and Bolton, Captains Ridgway, Widdows, Thompson, Gooch, and Buckton,Sar- geon Gornall, and Actin.. Surgeon Watkins, and Quarter- master Hutchinson. 'The tand of the corps was under the leadership of bandmaster Armstrong, and their excellent playing was the subject of general comment. The annual dance given to the men and their friends took place at the Drill Rail on Monday evening, and was A success. Sergeant-Bugler Plinstsn acted as master of the ceremonies, and the band of the corps played for daucinsr. Pioneer Warburton gave satiefaction as caterer. Dancing was kept up until the early hours of Tuesday mornin,....

BREAKING A WIFE'S NECK.—On Tuesday afternoon John Wheatley bhepherd murdered his wife at Wellington by breaking her neck. He had been drinking heavily,and was apprehended in his house about an hour after ths deed. The hearing of the charges against three army con- tractors. at York Assizes, of supplying the Government with forage and meat de'ficient in quantity and quality was cancl.aded on Wednesday, a verdict of not guilty being returned.

div.head: TRIAL OF LOUIS RIEL.
div.p: TRIAL OF LOUIS RIEL.

REGINA, WEDNESDAY.—LOtaS Riel's trial for treason has been resumed here.. Ten witnesses, including General Mid- dleton, have been examined up to the present. There is a great mass of evidence against the prisoner, including docu• ments in his own handwriting. A wrangle ensued in coma between Riel and his counsel, the latter threatening to throw up the case. The court ruled that the counsel should con- tinue, and Riel ceased interrupting. ' THE CHOLERA. STILL INCREASING IN SPAIN.

MADRID, SIINDAY.—The official bulletin gives the totals for yesterday as 3,35@ cases and 1,115 deaths. The returns from Soria are still outstanding. MADRU3, I‘4o@rms.—The official cholera bulletin issued this morning reports that, according to returns already received, there were 2,488 cases and 879 deaths in Spain yesterday. The returns from several provinces, however, are incomplete. MADRID, MONDAY—Most Of the C 3909 in Madrid are traceable to the fugitives from Valencia, Murcia, and Sara- gossa. Nearly all cases occur in the populous quarters, where great overcrowding exists. In some places there are from 300 to 400 persons in one house, with a total absence

of sanitary arrangements. The authorities endeavour to remedy this state of things, but with little satisfactory result. Sanitary precautions meet with considerable oppo- sition amongst the lower classes.—Standard. MADRID, WEDNESDAY, 9 PM —Yesterday, according to the official telegrams published up to the present hour, the total number of cases of cholera throughout Spain was 2,316, and the deaths 855. DEATH OF CARDINAL NINA.

- - ROME, SENDAY.—Cardinal Nina, late Secretary of State of Leo XIII., died last night. tie was born in 1812, and , received the cardinal's hat in 1877. CONSISTORY AT THE VATICAN. ROME, MONDAY.—A Consistory was held at the Vatican ' to•day, at which the Pope, after pronouncing an allocution, elevated the following prelates to the cardinalate in the Order of priests, namely :—Dr. Moran, Archbishop of Sydney ; Mgr. Melchers, Archbishop of Cologne ; Mgr. Capecelatro, Archbishop of Capria ; Mgr. Battaglia', Archbishop of Bo- logna ; and Mgr. Schiaffino. Bishop of Viessa in Partibns. Mgr. Cristofori was created a Cardinal in the Order of Dea- cons. The names of two other ecclesiastics to be created cardinals were reserved by his Holiness in Petto. The Pope also nominated 18 archbishops and bishops, including Dr. Walsh, to the See of Dublin. TURKISH OBSTRUCTION TO BRITISH TRADE. CONSTANTINOPLE, FRIDAY,—The obstruction to British trade in the harbour continues. Dilaver Pasha, the Prefet Of the Porte, has been unsuccessful in his efforts to recover the nine lighters belonging to two British firms, and still detained by the Corporation of Lightermen Mahonadjis. The Corporation ef Hamals (public porters) have so far carried eheir point in not allowing the paid servants of the Economic Co-operative Society to deliver the goods, which have now to be handed over by the latter to the " harnals " for delivery. This question also remains in abeyance. Sir William White has succeeded in obtaining from the Porte a settlement of some of the private claims of British contractors, which have been outstanding for many years. div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

RUSSIA AND ENGLAND. !CALCUTTA, SUNDAY—The Times of India publishes telegram from Meshed stating that the Russians have crossed the Hen i Rod at Pui-i-Khatun, and occupied some Persian territory, taking possession of a caravaeserai near the river, and of a position ten miles inland. It is added that a severe epidemic is causing great mortality 'among the Russian troops at Penjdeh. SATURDAY.—The Ameer of Afghanistan, on re- ceipt of the Empress of India's firman conferring upon his Highness the Grand Cross of the Star of India. or- dered a salute to be fired of 101 guns. Cabul was illu- minated on three successive nights, and copies of the firman were conspicuously posted up in the city. Pro. carnation of the firman was also made throughout-Afghan- istan.

VIENNA, MONDAY.—The Political Correspondence of to- day states that, as the turning point of the Anglo-Russian difficulty is not to be expected until after the coming general election in England. M. de Giers will take six or eight weeks' leave of absence, and will shortly proceed to Franzansbad.

BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.—lnformation received from St. Petersburg states that Russia by no means claims the Zul- fear Pass ; but insists upon retaining the adjoining territory as absolutely necessary for the security of her communica- tions with Akrobat and the pasture lands. It is added that this territory forms the sole question in dispute, and that it can only be settled by the manifestation of a conciliatory spirit on the part of England and Afghanistan.
