-- less girls into private houses—the haunts of wealthy scoundrels, who do not mind what they pay so long as there is constant and ua- failing provision for their criminal gratifica- tbn. What care these men in high places how soon the child they have seduced gravi- tates to "the streets I" They would smile to see keepers of common brothels caught in the net, knowing that with such a mesh as it had it would never hold the procuresses who were favoured with their patronage. The net must, therefore, be widened, and its meshes narrowed; it must reach the fashionable as well as the unfashionable haunts of vice; or the cry will still go up that there is one law for the rich, and another for the poor, and may be followed by such action on the part of a justly indignant people as wll shake society to its foundations. The masses bear many burdens, but there is a burden which they will not bear; they will not bear to see their daughters snatched from their hands to minister to idle debauchers who screen them- selves behind the law. Mr, FRANCIS PEAKE tells us that over 1,000 children have already been bought and sold in that secret market which is worse than a slave market, far the slave has at least a chance of escaping pollu- tion. We are horrified when we hear of the score or so of victims who are sacrificed at the death of an African King ; but there are hundreds being sacrificed nearer home,, and the time has come to make an effort—a persistent and continuous effort—to enchain or destroy the monsters that devour the children of Modern Babylon.

LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL is beginning to reap where he has sown. He has scat, tered the wild oats of politics, and he is now having an awkward crop. He should have attended a great Tory demonstration in Liverpool on Wednesday evening; he was " billed" as the greatest performer of the day ; the Circus was got ready, and there was no question as to an audience; but at the last moment he sent word that he could not be present, and he did not even say that he had the toothache or a sore throat. He found, it would appear, that he was likely to have a lively time of it—that there was some risk of his being hooted as well as cheered by local Conservatives; and as the Tory members for Liverpool, Lord CLAUD HAM rt.zorr and Mr. WHITLEY, were to be con- spicuous by their absence, he had a fit of " funk," or of sulk," and declined to perform. It transpires that the Conser- vative members for Liverpool are like many of their constituents, Conservative as well as Liberal, in thinking that the Gov- ernment have degraded themselves by eating their own words in the matter of their lush policy. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has been the chief sinner in this respect, and it is in harmony with the eternal fitness of things that he should be the chief sufferer. Some time ago when he was delighting a Tory audience by denouncing Mr. GLAD- STONE'S Government, he said :—" This is the school which bargains for Parliamentary support with the assassins of Phcenix Park; this is the school which, in order to de- feat the Tory party, will join hands again with Mr. PAN ELL in his de- mand for the independance of Ireland." With these words ringing in their ears— words which Irishmen will do well to ponder when estimating the value of his lordship's friendship—the Orangemen of Liverpool were not disposed to countenance the political jugglery they have recently witnessed ; hence the determination of Mr. 'WHITLEY and Lord CLAUD HAMILTON to stay away from the meeting; and hence the collapse of the de- monstration. The organ of the Liverpool Tories blames " all the persons concerned for what it describes as "the fiasco ;" but it seems to us that the borough members have shown courage and good sense in declining to bend the knee to Baal. If the Tories will remove the scales from their eyes and look to their idol they will find that " MARL - BORCIGH'S noble son" has feet of clay and a face of brass.

THE DEPUTY- CORONER held an inquiry on Monday afternoon into the circumstances of the death of JOHN LYNCH, a young militia- man, who was fatally injured at Warrington fair on the previous Thursday evening. The disclosures made as to the risks incurred in connection with the hobby-horses and swing- boats make it a matter of wonder, not that there is an accident now and again, but that accidents are not more frequent. Space is above all things necessary for the proper working of these machines, and it is obvious that there is too little space available on the ground used for the Warrington fair. We understand that the Corporation have the letting of the ground, and they can- not be held blameless if they allow it to be over-crowded. The young man LYNCH lost his life through falling out of a swing-boat ; but. it was not clear from the evidence whether he fell whilst attempting to stand up in the boat when it was in motion, or whether, as his companion asserts, they were both standing and swing- ing when the accident happened. The DEPUTY-CORONER did well to caution the man in charge of the boats against permitting persons to stand up in them. It is a most dangerous piactice, for it is notorious that the motion of a swing sometimes brings on a sudden sensation of faintness or sickness. It may be that, in the case of LYNCH, he lost his hold through faintness after swinging for a short time along with his comrade. It is very sad and shocking for a young man thus to lose his life in the hey-day of enjoyment. Those who attend fairs should profit by the lesson brought home to them, and proprietors of swing-boats &c., should be made to feel , that no avoidable risks are to be incurred--- that they are in fact held responsible for the prohibition of dangerous practices. WARRING-TON was all astir on Thursday night and last night consequent upon the news of the massing of the preamble of the Ship Canal Bill by the Committee of the House of Commons. The people who take an interest in this great project rightly, we believe, 'interpret the success which has so far attended the progress of the Bill as meaning that there is no risk now of its being rejected. Having, in the third attempt, safely " shot Niagara." they do not fear that it will triumphantly emerge from the smoother waters over which it has yet to mass. Hence the firing of cannon by way of salute, and the bfinging into requisition of bells, bands, and bunting. I The majority of the people of *this district have all along shown them- selves strongly in favour of the Bill, and. after the cup has been twice dashed from their lips, they may be excused if they are demonstrative when they are about to drink to their fill. The making of the Canal cannot fail to be beneficial to residents all along its line. Five or six millions of money cannot

be spent on the projcct without a ccy'r.- isiderable portion of it finding its way into the pock'ets of the people of Run- corn. Widnes, Warrington, and Man- chester. If they cannot rejoice at the prospect, we do not know who can. So far as the promoters are concerned, it will be noted that they have still some uphill work before them. The decision of the Commons' Committee is not one which errs on the side of leniency. The Parliamentary deposit is impounded, and besides raising a million in cash before beginning the work, the sum of one million and three quarters is to be obtained for the purchase of the Bridgewater and Mer- sey and Irwell Navigation. But the pro- moters are energetic men ; they have faced • " fearful odds " in presenting the Bill for three years in succession. The Chairman, Mr. DANIEL ADAIvISON, is bad to beat. Having pulled through so far, we hope he will be successful to the end, and that , his most sanguine expectations will be rea- lised.

Father Henry, S.J., preached two sermons in St. Michael's Church, Ditton Hall, on Sunday, before large congregations. Collections were taken in aid of the schools. Selections from "Carmen 'and " Patience " were played, and thoroughly enjoyed by a large assembly. Shooting took place at 200, 500, and 600 yards rabges, and B Company was victorious by 656 points to 643. . MAD DOG AT WlDEl2B.—Richard Great, caretaker of the Warrington-road Board Schools, on Saturday night killed a retrieeer dog, stated to be suffering from rabies. The ani- mal had attacked several persons, but fortunately without inflicting any injuries. ST. LUKE'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—Tbe annual services took place on Sunday, when the Rev. T. Flatlet Williams, of Buckley, preached morning and evening in Bethesda Chapel. In the afternoon a children's service was conducted at St. Luke's. The collections amounted ro £B. EXTENSIVE ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN.—Before kr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Thomas Valentine, a tramp, was remanded on a charge of stealing a pair of clogs from the works of Mr. T. Norman, earthenware pipe manufacturer, Runcorn. P.C. ,Harper apprehended the prisoner. with the clogs which be- long to a young man named Matthews, in his possession. Superintendent Leah said there had been extensive rob- beries of tools and clothing from this place. THE RUNCORN SMELTING COMPANY.—On Tuesday, at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, Messrs. Bateson and Co., 'elicitors. Castle-street, acting on behalf of a creditor, lodged a petition against John Hallows, of Alexandra. buildings, Ormond-street, Liverpool, trading as the Rune ,rn Smelting Company, and residing at the Farm, Ditton, flair Liverpool. '1 he petition was heard by Mr. Registrar Bellringer. and the debtor, who was repmsented by Mr. Charles Collins, consented to a receiving order being made. The public eximination was fixed for the 10th August, at twelve noon, in the. Court House, Victoria-street, Liyer- p 01. SHOCKING OUTRAGE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, John Fox, a chemical labourer living, in Viaduct-street, %sae 'charged with having, on Saturday night, committed a rape upon Martha Johnson, aged 11, who lives with her parents at 17, Vraductmtreet. —lt appeared that about eight o'clock on Saturday night Mrs. Johnson left the house for about a quarter of an hour. In her absence the prisoner entered by the back door and car- ried the girl into the bedroom of his own house, where he committed the offence with which he is charged. In reply to P.C. Evans, who apprehended him, he admitted his guilt.—The prisoner was remanded until Tuesday. A VIOLENT SON AT RUNCORIC—Joseph Dagdale, a young man, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, charged with assaulting his father, William Dugdale, of Halton.—The prisoner pleaded guilty. He said he struck his father because he was making faces at him. If he would kep his face straight he would not touch him. He treated the other lads like angels, but for him he had nothing but ugly faces to pull. His father said he dare not strike him, and "he put that on one side and did do." —The father said the prisoner struck him on the face. His conduct was so violent on some occasions that he was afraid be would murder him.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's bard labour. FRAITDULENTLY REILOVING GOODs.—James Lawton, a middle-aged man, residing at Widnes, was summoned at the Town Hall, on Friday, to show cause why he should not be committed to prison on a judgment summons for fraudulently removing his goods, at the instance of Mr. William Kitchen rent agent, St. Helens. On the 9th of January the defenClant was ordered to pay £7 8. for remov- ing his goods while owing rent, but he hid failed to do so. Mr. Kitchen said the defendant had been working at Widnes, and had promis-d to ply 3i par week. The defendant said he had been in search of work at Newton, Eerlestown, Pres- ton, and Wigan, but was unsuccessful. He had no means to pay at present. The case was adjourned. The rope was taken from the flat Inflexible on the 15th July, and on Tuesday last the prisoner sold it to Mr. Sprosten, the marine store dealer. Hr wan apprehended by P.S. Walley, and was now sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. ATHLETIC SPORTS AT RUNCORN.—The first of a series of athletic sports which the members of the Runcorn Football Club have decided to hold during the slimmer season took place on Saturday afternoon in A field adjacent to the High- field Tannery, Runcorn. The events were confined to members of the foot- ball club, but on future occasions they will be thrown open to the district, comprising Runcorn, Weston, and Halton. SWINE FEVER.—The " London Gazette.' contains a Privy Council order, notifying that the area com- prising the township of Widnes and the adjoining township of Ditton, in the county of Lancaster, which was declared infected with swine fever on the 30th of March last, is now free from such in- fection. • _ _ _ . _

JOSEPH MAZZINI, a memoir by E. A. V., with two essays by Mazzini : (1) "Thoughts on Democracy;' (2) The duties of man." No pecuniary profit is desired from this publication; but it is hoped that this eloquent memorial of anoblepatriot and a good man may awaken a true patriotic enthusiasm in the hearts of many young English readers ; and that the principles set forth may help to the forma- tion of wise and just political opinions. People's edition, with portrait, price 6d. To be obtained from JOHN S. GREEN, bookseller, &c., 34, Bridge- street, Warrington.—Advt. BURTONWOOD. On Monday the inhabitants of Burtonvvood had a good opportunity of visiting New Brighton. The trip, which has become an annual affair, was originated and planned by the popular vicar of the parish, the Rev. W. Wilson, and as usual this year the arrangements were car- ried out by the rev. gentleman. Leaving Collins Green about 9-30, the "trippers," to the number of about 120, reached New Brighton in due course, about 11 o'clock, when they dispersed to enjoy themselves after their own individual fashion. The weather was delightfully fine, and after a most en- joyable day the party reached Collins Green about 9-20 p.m. MR. GLADSTONE AND HIS SERVANTS.—Speaking at a meeting at High Leigh in support of the can- didature of Mr. John Brooks, a Mr, Carter, who 'was introduced as a Conservative working-man from Manchester, "criticised the acts of the late Govern- ment, and took occasion to remark that Mr. Glad- stone, whom he styled the "Green Old Man," had none but Roman Catholic servants on Hawarden estate. Considering that Mr. Gladstone was in the habit of reading the lessons in the parish church, he' thought the maintenance of these Roman Catholics was not only inconsistent, but perni- cious." Regarding it as absurd that Mr. Gladstone would make a. distinction ' either in favour of or against Roman Catholics, Mr. George Holford wrote to him and has received the following reply : " 1, Richmond-terrace, Whitehall, July 29th, 1885. Sir, I am di- rected by Mr. Gladstome to acknowledge the re- ceipt of your letter of the 27th inst., and to say that there is no truth whatever in the absurd state- ment to which you draw his attention. The proper course is to ask those who make these mendaciou accusations what their authority is for them.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, G. W. SPENCER LYTTLE- TON. Mr. Geo. Holford." The." div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

WIDNES THEATRE ROYAL.-0a the application Of Mr. George Mellor, the proprietor, a licence to perform nage plays was granted to the Theatre Royal, Wellington-street, by the Widnes magistrates on Wednesday. Messrs. T. Edwardson and James Chadwick were the sureties for the applicant. A GALL eNT WIDNES Boy—While the boys of the Wid- nes School Board were in the baths, on Saturday morning, one of their number, George Hughes, of Princess-street, was seized with cramp, and was in danger of being drowned. A boy named Clarkson, son of PS. Clarkson, pluckily jumpsd into the water and swam with Hughes to a place of safety. CAMDEN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—This building was well filled on Sunday afternoon, on the occa- sion of a flower service, which was conducted by the super- intendents. The rostrom was very tastefully decorated wil h plants and flowers from the conservatories of Mrs. C. Hale- burst, of Halton Grange. The Rev. Thomas Hackett de- livered an address upon flowers. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES —Mrs. MaXiVell, wife of a chemical labourer, living in Oxford-street, died suddenly on Monday afternoon. Three weeks ago she was confined, and no the afternoon in question she complained of being faint. r. McCarnbridge and Dr. McLennan were sent for, but death had taken place before thu arrival of the latter gen- tleman. Heart disease is supposed to be the cause of death. "TREATS" AT WIDNES.—On Saturday afternoon about 120 children belonging to the Parish Church Bind of Hope spent a pleasant afternoon in lisle Park. The C.E.T.S. brass band added considerably to the attractions. On the same afternoon 300 members of the " Sunbeam " Juvenile Temple of Good Templars travelled to Hough Green by train, accompanied by about 120 friends, and the Soap Works Bind. Mr. J. Longton had kindly placed a field at the disposal of the Temple, and an enjoyable time was spent. Tag COLLISION IN THE BRISTOL CHANNEL —Some de- tails of the terrible collision in the Bristol Channel, between the Cheerful and H.M.S. Heel i, have been furnished by one of the paesengers' who has returned to his home at Widnes. He relates also what may be considered a rather singular incident, that on Monday morning 13 passengers left the steamer at Plymouth on account of the rough passage they had from London to that port ; on Monday night 13 passengers sat down to tea, and there were 13 persons drowned. BETHESDA SCHOOL TREAT, RUNCORN.—On Tuesday morning about 600 scholars, teachers, parents, and friends connected with the Bethesia Sunday School were conveyed by boat along the canal to Keckwick, the occasion being the annual treat to the children. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, and the Rev. T. Hallett Williams, of Buckley, and the officers of the school were present, The weather was beautifully fine, and a most enjoyable fifiy was saent in a field kindly lent by Mr. Bennett, farmer. All requisite re- freshments were provided for the children. SALE OF WORK LT WIDNES.—For the purpose of raising funds to provide the members of the 'I Lily" Juvenile Tem- ple 1.0.G.T. with a trip in the country, a sale of work was held in the Science and-Art Buildines, Major Cross-street, on Saturday afternoon. There was a fair attendance at the opening ceremony, which was performed by Mr. J. R. Hud• son. The stalls, which were well laden with a variety of articles, were presided over by Miss Morewood, Miss Lamb, Mrs. Elewsona, Mrs. Butler, and Messrs. Widdows, Webb, and Hewsorn. In the evening a miscellaneous entertain- ment was given under the presidency ef Mr. Hudson. NELSON-STREET BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN —About IGO members of this society, and 30 adults assembled in the schoolroom, on Monday evening, and sat down to a good tea, free of charge. Afterwards they formed into proces- sional order and, beaded by Messrs. Joseph Bazley, Peter Pendleburv, and John Withington, superintendent of the Sunday school, and the Camden Brass Band, they walked through the main thoroughfares of the town. Mr. Samuel Ingletield, the president of the society, acted as chief mare shall. On the way, stoppages were made at the residences of Mrs. John Hazlehuret, Mr. R. Handles, Mr. John Tim- perley, and Mr. J. Leah, the superintendent of police. The band played a tune at each place. SUICIDE AT FARNAVORTH.--:thl Monday. before Mr. Brig- house, coroner, an inquest was held at the Griffin Inn, Fern- worth, on the body of Peter Walton, formerly a watch- maker, but who recently has been following the occupationl of a labourer, and lived at 30, Derby-road, Farnwortb, near Widnes.—Evidence was given to the effect that at 8 30 on the night in 'question the deceased came home under the in- fluence of drink, but was not drunk. He did not speak to anyone, but went upstairs. Between 9-30 and 10 his daugh- ter went upstairs for some cotton, and on entering the de- ceased's bedroom she found deceased suspended by a cord from a nail in the wall. Re was quite dead. The jury were unable to agree upon their verdict, and the inquiry was adjourned • until Monday next. ADDVELT.OWS' ANNIVERSARY AT HALE.--011 Monday the anniversary of the Loyal "Ireland Blackburae" Lodge No. 1801, of the Independent Order of Oddfellows was cele- brated at Hale. About 60 of the members, wearing their regalia, headed by the Roughdales Brass Band and the elub's banner, marched in procession to the residences of the principal gentry of the neighbourhood. The mernb-rs then proceeded to church, where a sermon was preached by the vicar. Afterwards the members sat down to a dinner at I the Cock and Trumpet. The auditor's report showed that the society is in a most Satisfactory condition. The num- ber of members on December Ilth, 1885, was 169 worth of lodge, December 11th, 1883. £3,04.9 18s lid', total worth of lodge, December 9th. 1884, £3,130 2a 6d ; gained last twelve months, £lOO 3s 7d.

SWUKSITNO INSTRUCTION FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN AT WIDNES.—The suggestion of Mr. Glover, made at the last meeting of the Widnes School Board, that the scholars should have the privilege of learning to swim, has quickly borne frait. On Saturday morning nearly 400 children visited th,baths, Messrs. Gasket', Deacon, and Co. having reduced the price of admissiOn to one penny. Mr. Shone, of Simrds Cross School, had charge of 125 boys; Mr. Snoddy, of West Bank School. 90 boys.; and Mr. Hunter' of Warrington-road School, 50 boys; and these occupied the baths from nine o'clock to half-past ten. About 80 boys from Ct. Patrick's School then occupied the baths until twelve o'clock. It is intended to give the scholars of the 1 different edboola lectures on the movements in swimming. ' Until the end of the season the baths will be reserved for scholars from 9 am. to 12 o'clock on Saturdays. Headed by the Grafton-street Industrial School Band. Liverpool, and the lodge banner, about 130 members attired in regalia paraded the main thoroughfares, calling at the residences of Dr. McDonnell, the lodge surgeon, in Mersey road; of gro. Kent. PUBLICANS P,3OSECUTED AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr, W. Bankes and Mr. A. Thomas, Arthur Percival, landlord of the Prospect Inn, Weston, was charged with permittingr drunkenness. Win. Guy was charged with beink drunk on Ithe premises. Mr. J. B. Fletcher, of Northwich. appeared for Percival.—P.C. Wallace deposed to visiting the Prospect Inn at eight minutes to ten on the 17th Jalv to make coine inquiries respecting a burglary. Mr. Percival was oa his hands and knees behind the door picking up a bat which be' afterwards placed upon Gives head. Guy was standing at the bar drunk. After transacting his business with Mr. Percival, Wallace went into the bar and saw Guy, who was sitting between two men, drink a glass of beer. On leaving the house he saw Guy leaning against the wall, and his wife trying to get him home.—P.C. Breeze corroboratad.— Mr. Percival denied that he picked the hat up, and said that Guy was quite sober.—Guy, who walks in a peculiar fashion, and speaks in a thick husky fashion, stated that he only wont into the house at a quarter to ten, and his wife ordered two glasses of beer, one for herself and one for him. He was qaite sober.—Thomas Whitley, Thomas Walton, each stated Guy was sober. The latter, in reply to Super:nten- dent Leah, said when Guy had had a glass or two he would lead folks to believe he was drunk. THE SHIP CANAL BILL
DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINUTON,

Last evening a large demonstration was held at Warring- ton in connection with the general rejoicings at the pass- ing through committee of the preamble of the Ship Canal [ Bill. Alderman Burgess and Dr. Mackie, who have been in London as a deputation from Warrington, were met at nine [ o'clock, on their return home, at Bank Quay Station, where several thousands of people had assembled. The deputation and others interested in the mattcr seteed them- , selves in two open landaus and a proccsssiou was formed. Headed by a band and a number of torch beirers, it pro- cesded through the main streets of the town to the Drill Hall, where a mass meeting was held and a congratulatory resolution passed. Jubilant speeches were made and much enthusiasm was manifested.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNE?_.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNE?_.

When the news of the decision of t—he—co.mmittee upon the Ship Canal scheme was received in Runcorn on Thurs- day night there was great rejqicing. People were grouped in the streets discussing the matter in an animated fashion, and from several places in the town cannons were fi,ed for a considerable time, netablv at the establishments of Mr. Timmins and Mr. Lea. Jemmy Erinshaw " was even 1 reaping a harvest through the glti tidings. On Friday morning he was walking through the street shouting in stentorian tones "rhyme" of his own composition. /ten- dered generous through the good news many people who have perhaps never given Jimmy " a penny before in their lives threw him a copper. Widnes was very little affected at the tidings. lhe canal is to run on the opposite side of the river, and it is generally regarded that whilst Widnes trade will not be benefited, the approaches to the docks may be blocked by physical altera- tion of the bed of the river,. but the Local Bard having fully secured the interes.te of the town, the inhabitants look upon the matter with a somewhat indifferent eve. YE•3IERDAY'S PROCEEDINOS.—COM Mil TEE'S DECISION AS TO THE DEPOSIT.

Mr. Forster's committee met Yesterday to consider clauses. —Mr. Pember at once asked the committee not to insist upon papunging.clause 42, which proposed to liberate the Parliamentary deposit of £276,000. If the deposit was im- , psunded, the sum of £276,000 would be locked up for seven l years. At the ordinary rate of interest that would involve la loss of £37,500 in the seven years.—Mr. Littler, on be. halhof Sir Humphrey de Trafford, opposed the excision of the clause on the ground that it was necessary for his pro- tection. The Chairman asked whether the Parlia- mentary deposit could be reckoned as part of the £1,000,000 which was to be raised in cash apart from the Bridgewater Canal purchase money before the works were commenced. —Mr. Littler raid he was informed there would be no diffi- culty about this.—Mr. Pember said that unless the pro- moters bought the Bridgewater Canal they could not turn Ft a sod ; in fact, the whole bill was useless until he got the , Bridgewater Canal in his hands.—After a short consulta. lion the committee decided to impound the deposit for three yeas, an announcement which gave entire sat;sfaction to 1 the promoters. The committee then proceeded to go through the clauses of the bill seriatim. Clauses one and two were agreed to without alteration. Clause three, which defines the part of Manchester, was 'es, consent altered so as to define the canal as so much of the navigable waters of the Mersey and Irwell as lie batwees Hunt's Bank in the parish of Manches- ter and the limit of part of Liverpool at Warrington.—Mr. Bidder next asked the committee to insert a clause in the bill prostosing an addition to the nominal capital of the company, mating tho shares £l6 instead of £lO, it being understood that the call should not be made except to make good any damage which might accrue from the works. The learned counsel further asked the committee to insert a clause providing that at any time during the progress or within 25 years after the completion of the works' the ol Mersey Docks and the Corporations of Liverpo and Birken- head should have power to demand an inquiry as to where the works had directly or indirectly caused, or where likely to cause, an injury, such inquiry to be referred to three referees appointed by the complainants,one b - the Sie:p Canal Company, and one by the Boat d of Trade.—The Chairman said he did not think it would be possible to give these clauses, as they would pat the canal entirely at the mercy of the Mersey Deck Board,— Mr. Michael also opposed the proposal to increase the capital for the purpose of providing for any possible damage. He said: I cannot consent to anythins of the sort. The sole object Is to prevent the possibility of carrying out the undertaking.—The Chairman said the Committee were con- vinced that if any injury were done the works could be re- Imoved from the estuary at a cost of a few thousand pounds. I—Mr. Michael: A. few tens.-The Chairman : The promoters I estimate that the cost of the canal will be £7,300,000, and we think that the case would be met by inserthaz a provision that of the £5,000,000 capital, £250,000 was riot to be called up for five years after the completion of the Works.— Mr.' Bidder said this was so small a sum that it was not worth while altering the bill.—Tbe material alterations pro- posed by the opponents were therefore abandoned—The 22nd clause was, at the imtance of Mr. Bidder, amended, so as to make the purchase of the Mersey and Trweil and, Bridgewater undertakings by the promoters coMpulsory.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO VAT ITER, • SCANNELL, OF WARRINGTON,
div.p: PRESENTATION TO VAT ITER, • SCANNELL, OF WARRINGTON,

On Sunday evening a presentation of an aditefk; of wel- come and a gold Cross of the League was presented to their chaplain (Father Scannell) by the members of the Cetholic Total Abstinence League of the Cross. Tnere was a large attendange. Mr. D. Houghton read the address, which was as follows :—" An address of welcome to Father Scerinell, 0.5.8 —lt is the wish of the council and every member of the League of the Cross to present von, dear Rev. Father Scannell, this eveeing, with the Cross of the League and an address to welcome you back home again. In . thie addre . ss there is expressed our feelings of Joy P. 'e,ttg you onto more in our midst occupying, as before, the position of chaplain of the League. Though. yo.w have teen absent only for a.. few weeks yet to us the time has eeenied long. The reason of this is obvious; for you being our guide, our leader, and, we may say, the chief cause of the life and soul of our society, your absence for a short time, has, so it were, made the society only half alive. Duane yonr absence we have felt like soldiers in the time of battle without our I general, and who have to keep up the fight in spite of his absence, for, as it is the Office of a general to instil courage and nerve into his soldiers be his own bravery, conduct and encouraging words, so, dear Rev. Father', by your leadership, your advice, and , your encouraging words, are led on with greater courage and nerve te fight for the great cause of temperance. We feel more confident. of success in our battle when we see you at our head. welcome back again, then, dear Rev. Father, yes, doubly welcome.. our only hope is that you have benefitted your health by your well-earned rest. May we, by our conduct and loyalty to- wards the society of which you are the chaplain, win in the future, as we hope we have done in the past, your coefi- nence and your affection We ask you to relative this emblem of the League and address, and frequently to glance over them in order to prove to you our loyalty anti sincerity ,as the chaplain of the League o/ thee Craw— -1 Warringtoe, July 26th, 1885.—Signed, D,. Houghton (President), T. Indgallon. (Vice-President),. 3. Mullins (Cor. Secretary), D. Connor (Financial Secretary)e) Father Scannell, in acknowledging the gift, said inagmuch as he was unconscious of having attempted or achieved any thing beyond the ordinary duties of chaplain to the League, he must conclude that their presentation to 'atm that 4hec.. ing was not so much an acknowledemen: of the services he might have rendered in promoting the interests and welfare of the League, but rather as a memorial of their undeviating kindness and goodwid towards him att their chaplain. They had made allusion to his labours in Connection with the League, but he could assure them that if thete had been any labour it had been a willing and cordial labour—a labour of love; and eas such he had locke.d forssrd to no other reward than thee promceion of their welfare and the advance of the grand and sacred cause of temperance. (Applause.) He ceold 'assure them that he felt mere than amply rewarded when he saw some wretched hovel of poverty, enieerr, and I not unfrequently vice, transformed by their, kiedge of total abstinence into e home of comfort and peace sod holy jay. As they had mentioned in their beautifed addrese, it WRS a welcome home to Father Scannell, a testimony of goodwill and loyalty on behalf of the members of the League towards their chaplain. They had likewise apreesed a,visle that the object of his holiday had been enained in recruited health and strength, and he was happy to be able to tell them that he returned home to pursue with renewed v;gour and fresh ardour his labours in Warringten—Keuo_ard he made an offering of the first fruits of hie restored health and strength to the members of the League of the Cress. (Clieers.)—Father Scannell then Bdt/think:red the pledge, and the meeting was brought to a clop.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Councillor

Greening. DRUNICENNESS.—Jarnes Ward and Ann Massey were each fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly on Friday nigilt. DasErrrna.—Jarnes Manning, who almitted being a deserter from the 4th Battalion York Regiment of Militia, was remanded till Monday. DEFRAUDING TILE RAILWAY COMPANY.—John Quinn, who stated that he lived at 7, Cab-street, off Deansgate, Manchester, was charged with riding from Liverpool to Warrington on the C'aeshire Lines, wilbout having paid his fare. It was stated that on the previous evening the pri- soner was found by a ticket-collector hiding under a seat in the 8 33 express, and en being drawn out it was found that he had no ticket. —Re was fined 10 and costs and also ordered to pay the railway fare from Liverpool to Warring- ton, or in default fourteen days' imprisonment. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), and

Councillor Greening. MISCELLANSOUS —The following were dealt with for drunkenness :—Sarah Ellen Wilkinson, in Dutton-street, on Saturday night, sent to prison for seven days; Margaret Burke, in Dial-street, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs; William Lloyd and Joseph Neale, in Pierpoint-street, on Sunday morning, fined 53 and costa each; Michael Dowd, in Old-road, Latchford, on Monday morning, fined 5s and costs • Mie,ael Rogerson, in Bridge-street, on the 21st July, fined 53 and costs; William Parker, in Winwick- street, on the 22nd July, fined 4s, inclu ling costs; Eliza- beth Glover, in Bewsev-street, on the 21st July, remanded in custody until the following clay.--James Mannion, charged with !ping an absentee from Her Majesty's 4th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment of . Militia during the recent training, was remanded.—Edward Connor, in an ad- journed case, was charged with keeping pigs in such a manner as to constitute a nuisance. He was ordered to abate the nuisance, within three days, subject to a penalty of lOs a day beyond that time, and to pay the costs of the case.—Jarnes Newton, charged with allowing two horses to stray, was ordered to pay costs.—Henry Oakley was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch-rod for throwing stones in Lil ford-street. ASSAULTING A 'Bus DRlVEEL—Patrick Fallon was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street on Sunday night, and with assaulting John Durnbell, a 'bus driver in the employ of the Warrington Carriage Company. Prisoner, because the driver refused to allow him to ride on the 'bus, struck him a violent blow on the face, He was fined 203 and costs, or a month's imprisonment. TUESDAY.—Baore Councillor Greening and Mr. E. J.

Guest. MISCELLANEOII3.—Eizabeth Glover, for being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street on the 201 a ult., was fined 10s end costs, and Margaret Trusselow, a respectably-dressed woman, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly in Scotland-road on the previous evening.—John Whitaker, a lad, was sant to prison for fourteen days for playing at pitch and toss ia Museum-street on the previous evening. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Pickmere. MascEr...Learnous.—Thomas Flynn, labourer, was fined 10s and costs for Wog drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street the previous evening, and for being guilty of a similar of- fence in Winwick-street, Samuel Handley was fined 5s and costs.—Randall Hamill, last from Liverpool, admitted de- serting from H.M. Royal Irish Rifles, and was remanded to Walton to await an escort.

FRlDLY.—Before Captain Reynolds (in the chair), Mr. I John White, and Dr. Gorman. MISCELIANEOUS.—Joseph Tinsley, charged with commit- log a nuisance in Bank Park on the 21st July, was ordered to pay lie costs, or go to prison for seven days.—James Mannino, charged with being an absentee from H.M. York- shire Regiment of Militia during the recent training, was tined 40e, without costs, or an alternative of one month's imprisonment.--Margaret Guest, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Oliphant-street, was dismissed on promising to leave the town.—Bridget Lally and Ann 1 Mahar were sent to prison for a month for sleeping in an empty house without visible means of subsistence.-- Michael Costello was ordered to pay costs for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the sth April.—Mary Bennett was summoned for using malicious threats to Mary Ann Derby.—The case was dismissed.—John Lawton and I William Bamford were fined 5s and costs for being drunk ' and disorderly in Winwick-street, and Michael Gilligan was fined the same sum for drunkenness.--Ellen Connor, on Promising to amend, was dismissed on a similar charge. Kate Ratcliffe was ordered to pay costs for being drunk and disorderly on Pinners-brow.—John Nixon and William Richardson, summoned for fighting in Wiuwick-street, on the 25th July. were dismissed on paying costs.---Ellen McCormick (18), for using obscene language in Museum- street, on Thursday morning, was fined 59, including costa, or seven days' imprisonment. BREAKING INTO BARRACKS —Mary Ellen Keighley (18) and Caaherine Paul (17) were sent to prison for seven days as rogues and vagabonds, they haying been found in a barrack-room at Orford barracks at midnight. They said they had got over the wall, wkich is about 10 feet high, sod were assisted by three soldiers. A sergeant from the barracks said that the three soldiers would be punished by the commanding officer. WIFE DESERTION.—SamueI Tally was charged with de- serting his wife on the Bth July, and with being absent from the training of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Militia. Be deserted his wife three months after marriage, and she was several weeks ill in the Workhouse.—For the first offence he was sent to prison for a month, and for the second was lined 40s and costs, or a month's imprison- moot.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY—Before Mr. J. Brock. DRUNKENNESS —For this offence fines were impotked upon Owen Mularkey, Philip Murray, John Skalley, Mary Ann Walsh, Michael Walsh. Patrick Moylan, Patrick Leonard, and Patrick Cullen. For being drunk on the licensed pre- mises of Harris Tyrer, John O'Brien was fined lOs and costa.
BREACH OF THE PEACE —For making a disturbance in Dock-street, on Saturday, Joseph Furlong was bound over for two months.

The other youths escaped.—lnspector Wood said there had been nurnerons complaints that this game was a nuisance.—A fine of 2s Bd and costs was imposed. On Sunday night the prisoner created a disturbance in the Central Hotel, and he was ejected by Mr. Parkes. In the street his conduct was very noisy and violent, and P.C. Cummings, after a chase, took him into custody. The Prisoner threw the constable to the ground, bit his arm and kicked him, and also tore his trousers. DISORDERLY CHARACTERS —Louisa Spencer was sen- tenced to 21 days' hard labour on a charge of being guilty of disorderly cmduct in High-street on Saturday night.— Inspector Roche proved the case.—William Peck and James Shaw, young men, were sent to gaol for seven days, on the evidence of P.S. Neild, for sleeping in the outbuild- ings of the Egerton Arms Hotel on the 26th inst.

- , ALLEGED Ousrancrtme.—The case of an alleged obstruc- tion to the read by Jos. Smith, a farmer, again came before the bench. It was stated that after the case had been ad- journed at the last sessions, it came before the Highway Board, which had appointed a committee to meet Mr. Smith on the matter. It had now been settled, the obitrac- tion having already been partially removed. Under these circumstances Supt. Leighton withdrew the charge against mith. .

ASSAULT ON A GlRL.—Herbert Walker, 17, was charged with having assaulted and beaten Sarah Allen on the 3rd July. Mr. P. Davies defended. It appeared that both the complainant and defendant bad been servants with Mr. Brocklehurst, farmer, and on the day in question defendant knocked a little girl down who was playing with Mr. Brockleburst's children. The complainant interfered, when she was assaulted and knocked about rather severely. De- fendant was fined is. and costs,

~,.......---— DRUNKENNESS.—AIex4auer Beach and George Beach were fined, the former 7s 6d and costs and the latter 5s and costs, for being drunk and disorderly at Little Leigh on the 19th July. A BAKER Freren.—James Strange, a baker, Warrington, was fined 54 and costs for having allowed bread to ba de- livered without having a pair of scales in the cart, in Thelwall-road, Latchfo'rd, on the Bth inst.—Mrs. Strati4e, who appeared for her husband, said the boy who had charge of the cart had neglected to take the scales. MORE SWINE CASES.—Peter Stringer was charged with having removed two pigs from Warrington into Cheshire on the 17th July, in contravention of an order ; and Thomas Leach and Charles Rovlance were charged with a similar offence on the Bth July. Arthur Hodgson was charged with having allowed these pigs to be removed.—Stringer and Roylance pleaded guilty, they not having known that the order in question was in force ; Leach was discharged on it being shown that he bad not had a band In the removal. Hodgson, who is a railway labourer, living in Wilson- Patten-street, WAS the person who sold the pig., and it ap- peared that he had previously gone to Sergeant Booth, at Stockton Heath, for a licence to remove the pigs, but he was told by the sergeant that no licence could be given because an order had been issued prohibiting tie removal of any pigs into Cheshire for a certain period. This order was also read I over to the defendant. The latter, though he admitted that , the order was read over to him, pleaded that he understood' the order to mean that pigs could now be removed wipeout I I a licence, and had acted on that impression.—Rovlance and Stringer were Ordered to pay the costs, 8s 6d, and Hodgson ' to pay the costs on two cases, 17s. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—JOSeptI MOSS, James Wilkinson, land James Berry were each ordered to pay 5s in respect r 4 the irregular attendance of their chihlren at school. STEALING EGGS.—GeOrge Hatton, a boy belon.eing to Lower Walton, was charged with having stolen two eggs on the 27th July, the property of Henry Hallwood. Hatton, it seemed, was in the habit of sleeping out at night, and lead- ing a neglected life. On the day in question Mr. Hallwood caught him in the stable' and being asked what he was doing he replied that he had taken two eggs and had come , for two more.—He was committed to gaol for 14 days, and I ordered to be afterwards sent to a reformatory for four years.
HOW IT ACTS.

HELD DOW :r IN BED BY TWO MEN. Mr. Wm. Buchanan, No. 8, Bt. John's-road, %tradele, Liverpoot, has been an engiceer in the ' Cunard Pteamship Company's Service ,or twenty years. He states that for eighteen months he was troubled with most distressing neuralgic pains in his head. The most eminent physicians, although united as Co the cause, could not afford relief, and declared his case incurable. He resigned his posi- tion on account of his sufferings, and at last, on the advice of his friends, tried St. Jacob's Oil. The first bottle, he says, gave him great relief, and the second cured him. He is now following his employment, and is as well as aver. This remark- able statement is endorsed by Mr. Joseph Gill, Manager for Messrs. Sudden and Co., chemists, No. 399, Stanley-road, Liverpool. div.head: EDUCATION ACT.-IMPORTANT DECISION.
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT.-IMPORTANT DECISION.
Al

Mr. George Riley, School Attendance Offi 3er, ap • peared to prosecute at the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, in a number of cases in which parents were summoned for neglecting ti send their children to school. When the cases were called on a decision of some importance to parents was referred to, and Mr. Riley handed in a report of it, which read as follows: A decision of great importance to all con- nected with school boards was given in the Court of Queen's Bench on Thursday, July 2nd. The point was as to what constituted an attendance at school under the Education Acts. A parent sent his child to school without a fee. The child was admitted and allowed to attend the school, bat the parent was, nevertheless, summoned for the non-attendance of his child, the School Board holding that payment of the fee was necessary to constitute the attendance of a child at school an attendance under the Act. The magistrate refused to convict, but stated a case for the decision of the higher court. This decision was given in favour of the School Board. The Lord Chief Justice held that the parent had not caused the child to attend school within the meaning of the Act, and Mr. Justice Grove, Mr. Justice Denman, and Mr. Justice Mathew concurred with the opinion expressed by Lord Coleridge. It follows that School Boards have now a ready means of enforcing payment of school fees, while the child does not suffer eaucation- ally. He may attend school and receive the benefit of the instruction there given, and yet the parent may be fined for the technical non-attendance of his child." The following people were then fined se. each for the non-attendance of their children :—Mary Bennett, Pierpoint- street ; Samuel Carter, forgeman, ' D allam-lane ; John Daniels, (slogger, Greenall•street , Benjamin Matthewnian, wire weaver, Scott-street ; John Fillingham, forgeman, Daley-street; John Burgess, forgeman, Winwick-street ; Thomas Clark, carter, Manchester-lane; and Edward Cartwright, forgeman, Fennel-street. The following, who were each summoned with respect to two children, were fined !co?. :—Sarah Marsh, Hall-street ; Charles Cot- teril, forgeman, Lythgoes•lane ; Joseph Kirkham, forgeman, rierpoint-street ; and James Hughes, forgeman, Pierpoint-street. In nearly all the cases the attendance of the children had been bad and school money was owing.

WARRINGTON AND GROUND v. WERNETH AND GROUND. —This match was played at Warrington on Satardav, and resulted in a draw greatly in favour of the home team: War- rington won the toss, and went in on a good wicket. Runs came slowly at first, the bowling being excellent. Several stands were made, bat the score was not materially increased until the total was 72 for seven wickets. Armstrong and Jolley were now together, and, playing freely, put on runs at a great pace, Bates, Brelsford, Reggae, Woodhouse. and Cordwell in turn taking the places of Seaton and Hodkinson, and relieved each other in rapid succession, but to no pur- pose. Jolley was bowled at 127, and England stayed while Armstrong hit. At 195 England was bowled, and Smith made 16 out of the next 20. Armstrong was caught by Haggas after a brilliant innings of 82; he made one or two, fluky hits, but otherwise he hit very clean and hard. His score included thirteen 4's. The innings closed for 216 runs. The general fielding of the Werneth team was good, and Mavall at wicket was much admired for his smartness. Andrews and Haggas began for Werneth to the bowling of J. C. Lawton (medium right) and Smith (fast right). After being hit for ten runs in three flyers, the former bowled ten maiden ovens in succession for four wickets. Andrews only was able to play Smith confidently. The first hour's play produced 23 runs, of which five were extras. J. Walker and Woodhouse got together twenty minutes before time, and despite two changes were still together when time was called. div.head: GENERAL NEWS._
div.p: GENERAL NEWS._

REPRIEVE Or A --tIRDERESh.—A reprieve has been se ceived from the Hoene Secretary by the tle,-e.esor 1 Dur- ham. Gaol for Sarah Punn, Mears...et, svto wan sentenctel to death last Saturday by Stir. Justice Wills for the murder of her illigitimate child at Middridge, near Bishop Auckland. THREATENED WATER FAMINE AT LIVEEPOOL.—Liverpool is threatened with a water famine. The hot and dry weather has greatly reduced the amount in store, and already the supply to the inhabitants has been stopped for one half the day. Steps are being taken to water the streets with salt water, and to urge economy upon the out town- ships. DISGRACEFUL OUTRAGE.—Whippingbam Church was re- opened to the public on Sunday. In less than an hour after the Royal marriage a crowd of excarsionists forced their way into the church, and reduced the decorations to a total wreck. The delicate flowers were stolen or trampled under foot, and the whole agair was a disgraceful outrage. Bow FROM ENGLAND TO FRANCE —On Saturday morning the Oxford crew started in their boat from the Admiralty Pier, Dover, for a pull across the English Channel. There was scarcely a breath of wind, and the sea was quite smooth. When nearing Calais a chopping ripple was experienced,but no oars were broken during the trip,which was accomplished in four hours and a half. TERRIBLE YACHTING DISASTER.-013 the 13th ult, the steam yacht Minnie Cook, with ten persons on board, was cruising in Lake Minnetouka, United States, when a sudden and terrific storm burst over the water. The steamer was overtaken, and went down with all on board. The lake was subsequently dragged,and seven of the bodies recovered All the unfortunate people were well connected and much respected. MURDER OF A MOTHER.—At the Chester Summer Aseizes on Wednesday, a young farmer named James Horrabin was indicted for the murder of his mother at Buglawton on May 26. It was stated by two surgeons who had examined the prisoner that he was not in a fit condition to take his trial, and that, in fact, he was insane. The jury found a verdict to that effect, and Horrabin was ordered to be detained dur- ing her Majesty's pleasure. THE Crinuirrat Law AMENDMENT BlLL.—General Booth spoke at Leeds on Monday night in support of the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, so far as it affects the protection of young girls. He said the Mansion HOUSS Committee's ver- dict would vindicate the secret commission. Revelations more horrible than those that had been made remained un- told. Resolutions were carried approving the bill, and the proposed amendment raising the age for protection. DEATH FROM A CAT'S BITE.—An inquest was held in London on Tuesday, on the body of John Tittenson, aged 43 years. In March a black cat entered the deceased's house and bit his little daughter, six years „fold. Hearing the child cry, the deceased went to her aid, when the cat bit him on the left thumb. The cat was killed. The wound on Tittenson was cauterised, and he did not feel ill until last Friday. A verdict of "Death from hydrophobia" was returned. MUTINY AT AN INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.—An outbreak took place on Saturday night and Monday morning among the boys of Greenock Industrial School, and several of them have escaped from the institution. The cause of the revolt is alleged to have been the ill-treatment of the boys by the drillmaster and his wife, against whom a charge has been lodged at Greenock Police Office. The boys effected their escape by leaping from the windows aud thea scaling the walls, one or two being injured. A Timm ON FlRE.—About noon on Saturday, a goods train proceeding from Willesden Junction towards Chalk Farm, was discovered to be on fire while passieg through Queen's Park Station of the London and North-Western It tilway. The fire was burning in the centre of the train, where coins heavily-loaded trucks of hay were coupled. The fire had got a good hold on four trucks, which with their contents were almost entirely destroyed. It is supposed that the nre was caused by a spark from the engine, which ig- nited the highly heated hay. MILITARY RIOT.—At Colchester on Saturday, a serious riot took place between some soldiers and a number of civilians. A quarrel had occurred at the camp lines, when a civilian struck a sergeant of the military police, and was promptly knocked down in return. This led to the civi- vilians assaulting the military, and a general fight ensued, lasting nearly an hour. The soldiers used their belts, and the civilians their sticks and stones. An armed picket, with fixed bayonets, ultimately restored order Several of the combatants were seriously injured. PRINCE AND PRINCESS HENRY OF BATTENBEE.G. At Windsor Castle a suite of apartments is to be prepared fer the use of Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg when reseling at the Palace with the Queen. Apartments will likewise be provided for the Prince and Princess at Bal- moral when the court is in Scotland. There being a bal- ance of upwardakf £6B left of the funds subscribed by the residents of Widlisor and Eton for a wedding present for Princess Beatrice, it is proposed to expend the amount on the purchase of a silver bowl as an additional gift for her Royal Highness. A REMARKABLE THANCE —At Fardrurn, near Athlone. a young woman has recovered from a short but remark- able trance. Her friends, thinking her dead, had laid out the body, and owing to the suddenness of the event com- municated with the police, who wrote to the coroner for the purpose of holding an inquest. Subsequently, how-. ever, a friend of the family went to see the corpse, and ex- pressing an opinion that the girl, whose name is Brophy, was not dead, he lifted the body and shook it. Very shortly afterwards signs of animation were observed. Gradually the young woman regained consciousness, and is rapidly recovering. MINERS' DEMONSTRATION.—The miners of the county of Durham held their fifteenth demonstration on Saturday on Durham racecourse. Nearly 50,000 were present. Ad- dresses were delivered by Mr. Burt, M.P., Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., and Mr. Broadhurst. M.P. Referring to the state of trade, Mr. Bart declared that it was a misnomer to speak of it as depressed as far as the coal trade was concerned. He did not advocate an artificial limitation of production, but he did advocate that the men should take their brains into the pit with them and work in a rational way. If they cliol that there would not be a man out of employment in any pit in the kingdom. The hon, member dwelt upon the im- portance of considering coal dust as an element of danger in coal mines. They ought to demand better supervision, and that the checkweighmen should be better protected from the inroads ef the coalowners. A resolution was passed re- gretting the accidents at collieries at Usworth, Philadelphia, and Pendlebury, and calling for further legislation for the protection of life in mines, and expressing the meeting's entire approval of the bill introduced by Mr. Thomas Mut seeking to amend the Employers' Liability Act. ALARMING Pima DISASTER.—On Sunday afternoon the steamboat which plies between Strood and Southend called at Chatham Pier on the way down the river. A large num- ber of excursionists were waiting on the pierhead, and as soon as the vessel was moored alongside a stream of pas- sengers' passed through the barrier to descend to the lower tier of the pier by means of an iron structure, when, without a moment's warning, and at a moment when some seventy or eighty persons were on the structure, it col- lapsed, precipitating them into the river. An indescribable scene of excitement followed, as a large number of the In- tending passengers were women, who in many instances I were accompanied by children ; and it was only by the exercise of considerable promptitude and skill that the boatmen at the pierbead managed to thread their boats through the entanglement of the broken iron and wood- work and rescue any persons from the struggling maw A large number of those who were saved sustained fractured limbs.. Several women were taken to the Sun Hotel close by, half drowned and in an unconscious condition. The pier had been in course of reconstruction. The catastrophe has cast a deep gloom over the town, and the boat service was suspended. Against all expectations only one death has occurred. It is that of an infant which was struck on the head by a piece of iron. MR. FORSTER,. M.P., ON THE SOUTH AFRICAN qUESTION. —The South African Cemmittee and the Committee of the Aborigines Protection Society entertained a party of gentle- , men interested in the affairs of Bechuanaland and ZUluland ' on Saturday in London. Mr. W. E. Forster, M.P., presided. He said that never at any time had the affair of South Africa been in a more critical position than at the present moment. It was generally admitted, he believed,teat Sir C. Warren's mission had been a great success. The gallant officer had restored peace and order, had asserted the rights of the natives, had vindicated the claims of justice, and bad done much to prevent aggression and robbery hereafter. ' (Hear, hear.) There had been, unfortunately, some differ- ences of opinion between Sir C. Warren and Sir Hercules Robinson; but they all trusted that those diffsrences would not lead to auy alterations of policy, and above all, to the admission that the Queen's authority was not to be respec- ted in South Africa; but that wherever that authority was in force it should mean the prevention of ininstirm.r and the protection of all classes—be they white or black. In regard to Zululand, he asserted that if the English Government were to recognise the filibustering Republic of the Boers Ithe sooner we left South Africa the better ; for it would simply mean the Government of half a million of people by a small oligarchy of white men.' DEATH or SIR MOSES Morovvvronp.—Sir Moses Monte- fibre, Bart., expired at half -past four o'clock on Tuesday, afternoon. His death was not unexpected, although when it did come it was somewhat sudden. Considering his ad- vanced age—nearly 101 years—he has enjoyed most remark- ably robust health, and it was only some nwe. or three days ' ago that he was seen to be breaking up. The deceased baronet was bore October 24th, 1784, and was the son of the late Joseph Monttfiore, Esq. In 1837 be held the Offiea of Sheriff of London, and was knighted on the visit of her Majesty to the Guildhall, on November 9th of that year. He has been High Sheriff of Kent, in which county he re- sided, and was reised to a baronetcy in 1846, in recognition of his high character and public services. In 1867 he weal successful in a mission to Bournelia in favour of his op- pressed brethren in that country. Sir Moses founded, in 1867, a Jewish college at Ratnsgate, in memory of his wife, Judith, Lady Montefiere. On the occasion of Sir Moses] Montefiore celebrating his hundredth birthday there were great rejoicings at Ramsgate, where he dwelt. At the same ' nine his great worth was acknowledged thronghodt the civilised world. One of the last, if not the last, administra- tive acts of the deceased was to sign the cheque for the pur- chase of a cabinet which he presented to the Princess Bea- trice on her recent marriage, in bed, propped up with pil- lows. The title dies with the deceased, he being childless. The deceased baronet leaves numerous nephews and nieces, and it is believed that his residuary legatees will be his two nephews, Mr. Joseph Sebag and Mr. H. Cruedella, both of whom were with him duriug his last hours. It is estimated that the deceased baronet's estate will realise about anc million sterling.

FLOWER SHOW AT LATCHFORD. I The Cotrunittel of the r.eteheeea mee-.1 Society herd tbtor annual flower show on Saturday in the National School, Wash-lane, Latchford. The society in pre- vious years has had very good, though email, exhibitions, and this year competition was extended tee Grappenhall, St. James's, and Stockton Heath parishes, with very satis- factory results. The Vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescott, had worked assiduously to promote the interests of the society, and a committee, with Mr. William Wallace as honorary secretary, ably took the work in hand. In addition, the gentry residing in the- competing parishes gave their aid, and Mr. McMinnies, M.P., and Sir Gilbert Greenall were amongst those who gave liberal donations. The exhibition W 55 opened at noon, and was during the day inspected by a large number of people, who expressed flattering opinions of it as a whole, and of many of the exhibits in particular. The exhibits were excellently staged in the infants' schoO- reom and two adjoining class rooms, by Mr.Warkinson. Mr. Green, head gardener at Bank Park, Warrington, and Mr. Bolton, of Ackers-lane, Latchford, were the judges, and their awards were unquestioned and irapartial. During the afternoon and evening selections of music were played by St. Peter's Brass Band. Prizes were offered for cottagers' window plants, cut flowers, fruit, vegetables, and wild flowers exhibited by children. There was also a class for gentlemen and gardeners, another for amateurs, and extra prizes were offered for the most creditably kept flower gardens in Latchford and Grappenhall. Amongst the ex- hibits most worthy of notice were a tine collection of stove and greenhouse plants shown by Mr Lonsdale, gardener to Mr. Whitley, Stockton Heath; collections of cut rose blooms shown by Mrs. Litton, Mr. William Tinsley, and Mr Wright, London Bridge ; and a collection of stove and greenhouse plants exhibited by Mr. C. Broadbent. Mr. James Meredith, of Bridge-street, Warrington, had on exhibition two baskets of mushrooms and a quantity of mushroom spawn similar to that from which they were pro- duced. One basket contained mushrooms of extraordinary size, showing the strength of the spawn, and some of them were over lib in weight. In the other basket were placed four or five dozen mushrooms of uniform size and good sub- stance. They were grown by Mr. Joseph Meredith, of Fern Bank, Tirr.perley. The floral exhibits of Mr. Whitley and Mr. Appleton were much admired, and the garden de- signs of Mr. Wright came in for considerable notice. One great object of the society is, we believe, to encourage the cultivation of flowers and vegetables by the cottagers resi- dent in the neighbourhood, and their exhibits were an eloquent testimony-that the encouragement had been both 1 recognised and appreciated. Miss M. G. Taylor,of the Fire, Latchford, bad on view, not for competition, a ,box of fine second years' seedling potatoes, and the Liverpool horticul- tural Company, Gorgon, exhibited a collection of stove and greenhouse plants. div.head: LOCAL EMBEZZLEMENT CASE.
div.p: LOCAL EMBEZZLEMENT CASE.

At the Liverpool City Sessions, held on Saturday.before Mr. Sainuell, the Deputy Recorder, Frederick Augustus Harrison, 35 years of age, a commercial traveller, of re- spectable appearance' who some time ago was a relieving officer in the Prescot Union. was indicted on the charge of having, on the 15th of January, and other days being then servant to Henry Leo Stern, received and taken into his possession the several sums of £3 15s, £7 2s 6d, £l4 ss, £2, £4 7s 6d, and £5 5s 61, for and on account of his employer, and afterwards feloniously embezzled the same. Mr. Louis Williams prosecuted, and Dr. Commins, M.P., re- presented the prisoner.—From the opening statement of Mr. Williams it appeared that the prisoner was employed about 12 months ago by Mr. Leo Stern, who carried on the business of cigar merchant, South Castleestreet, Liverpool, and it was his duty to go about the country and seek for orders for cigars, collect the money outstanding, and every week hand over the amount collected to his employer. Pri- soner was paid half the profits of the business as a salary. Invoices were sent out to customers having business with the prosecutor, to which prisoner attached a printed form of receipt on settlement of any account. About the end of last month Mr. Stern communicated with a number of his , customers, and upon receivirg replies from them he spoke to the prisoner, informing him that several of his customers had denied their indebtedness to him, and asking for an ex- planation. The prisoner then said, "1 think I have re- ceived certain moneys that I have not accounted for, for the reason that I have used them in the business." He was afterwards pressed further, and upon being told that he would be charged he said, "Ibis amount I received was about £30." Later on the prisoner handed over to the pro- secutor a list of his deficiencies, and among other items re- ceived by him mentioned a sum of £l4, which was one of the items he was charged with embezzling. Prisoner was subsequently given into custody, and when brought before the magistrates and charged with embezzling the money he said, "Jam not guilty of embezzling : I used the money ,in the business." He (Mr. Williams) presumed that the deputy recorder would point out to the jury that a person , had no right to use large sums of money in the business of his employer without first letting him know that he was doing so.—Mr. Stern, the prosecutor, in corro- borating this statement, said that the deficiencies amounted to £157, but the accused, when spoken to about the matter, said the deficiencies only amounted to £3o.—ln re-examina- tion, the prosecutor said he paid the prisoner during the twelve months £167 in expenses and £7O in commission.— Witnesses were also examined as to their having paid to the prisoner sums of money which he never accounted for.— Dr. Comrnins argued that tho prisoner had undivided in- terest in the business, and he submitted there was no cri- retinal act on the part of the prisoner, who had absolute right to deduct his own commission from the amounts he 1 received—Mr. Williams contended that the prisoner could have no right to misinform his employer as to the moneys he collected upon the ground that he used it in the busi- ness.—Dr. Commins said the prisoner took no money but what he vas clearly • entitled to, and there might be now three times as much money owing to him as he had taken. A big business was being worked up by the prisoner, which he alleged Mr. Stern Wanted to confiscate by those cruel proceedings. After the deputy-recorder had summed no the evidence the jury returned a verdict of guilty, and pri- soner was committed to three calendar months' imprison- ment.

div.head: CORONERS' JURIES AND THEIR RIGHTS.
div.p: CORONERS' JURIES AND THEIR RIGHTS.

On Monday afternoon the deputy-coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband, held two inquests at the White Hart Hotel, Warrington, one being an adjourned one, and the same jury served for both. During the proceedings the fact that in the borough of War- rington no fees are paid to jurymen was referred to, and a juror stated that he had written to the editor of a Liverpool paper on the subject, the reply being that the proper course to take would be to commu- nicate with the Home Secretary. If a petition was drawn up and signed by that jury would, he asked, either Mr. Husband or Mr. Brighouse forward it to the Home Secretary ?—The Deputy-Coroner said that he, and Mr. Brighouse also, he was sure, would do anything they could to get juries paid. He thought it could be managed without troubling the Home Secretary. These remarks he based upon other districts, where fees were allowed. There should simply be a town's meeting called to con- sider the matter. He would render any assistance that he could.—A Juror : Is it competent for the warrant officer to warn myself, or any gentleman, on a jury at a moment's notice ?—The Dtputy- Coroner :—lt is competent for him to do so, and the law says he shall do so. Very often the officer him- self has no more notice than you have.—A Juror: Is not it necessary that you should be summoned and not told by word of mouth ?—The Deputy- Coroner replied that he did not think it was. If they were going to put the county to that expense he was afraid the county . would not agree to the payment of fees.—A iuror wished to mention a matter regarding which, he had no doubt, the majority of the jury would agree with him. In 19 cases out of 20 the juries were com- posed of one class—(a voice: "Publicans.")—" pub- licans and sinners.' He would like to ask the Deputy Coroner whether he thought that it was fair that one set of tradesmen should be called from business, when their time was quite as valuable to them as that of either a grocer, baker, or butcher? —The Deputy Coroner agreed that it was hard upon one class to be constantly drained to attend juries. There was no doubt that there were certian willing horses who were liable to be put upon. The police and publicans were so often associated together that the former always knew where they could get a willing horse. There were a certain class that the police did not, or dared not, trouble. They seldom saw any of the "upper ten" on juries, though there was no doubt they were equally liable to serve, and there was little doubt that if they were summoned there would soon be a certain allowance in fees. That was also a matter that rested in their own hands. If the jury were to write to the Home Sec- retary, or any individual upon the jury were to do so, and say that they were constantly being put upon coroners' juries, he had no doubt that some inquiry would be made, and the matter put right. The police had to act on instructions given to them, and if they were instructed to select jurymen with a little more discrimination, it would no doubt be done.—The subject then dropped.

Terrific storms are reported from the French provinces. At Rodetz the lightning set fire to a seminary and to several farms. Several persons are reported to have been killed. A supplementary estimate • issued on Thursday shows that an additienal sum of £5OO will be required for the erection of a monument to General Gordon in Trafalgar Square. • ZiMASHING A MAN'S RIBS.—A, man named Rowan was illtreating a woman in a low part of Limerick, on Satur- day, when another man named .L9rdan went to her assist- ance. Rowan thereupon attacked him, and it is alleged broke his ribs, so that his life is in danger. Rowan was arrested.

MANSLAUGHTER BY A BOIL—At Sheffield, on Tuesday, Samuel Yates, a lsd, was charged with manslaughter. Another lad, named Martin, was fighting with a boy the previous night. Yates rushed into the affray, and kicked Martin violenVy in the abdomen. Martin expired almost immediately. Yates stands tern anded. THE MUNSTER BANK —The Express says that the ab- sconding of Farquharson will give the coup de grace to the prospect of the resucitation of the Munster Bank. The Irish Times says that with such a state of facts it is prema- ture to discuss reconstruction The Freeman says that the disclosures will impede the efforts being made for recon- struction.

MR. GLADSTONE'S HEALTM—The following reply has been received in responss to a request that Mr. Gladstone should address a meeting of Welsh electors in South Glamorganshire:—" Sir,—Mr. Gladstone has revived your letter, which has been handed to him by Mr. Herbert Glad- stone. He fears that it will not he possible for him, under the circumstances, to pay a visit to Glamorganshire, both on account cf his existing engagements and the imperative orders he is under to spare his voice as much as possible. You have his heartiest good wishes for the forthcoming election.—Yours, G. W. SPENCER LYTTLETON.—Arthur Williams, Esq." . _

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
MONDAY.

At this—the 31st—siting—oilhe Select Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill the counsel for the oppo- nents began their addresses no the bill, the first to speak being Mr. Bidder, Q.C., representing the Mersey Cock and Harbour Board. The learned counsel devoted himself en- tirely to the engineering aspects of the case. He said there was an unconcealed anxiety to geta bill of some sort. This was" the third time of asking." An immense amonnt of money had been spent, great efforts bad been put forth, and to have to go back to Manchester with a third failure would naturally be felt by the promoters to be nothing less 1 than a discredit. It was not to be wondered at, under these circumstances, that the scheme should change from day to day. The present scheme. as he contended,.entailed serious and entirely gratuitous damage to the estuary. It was a scheme of the crudest and most undigested character, and would not have been pat forward by any person acquainted with the principles of hydraulic engineering that mast govern the case. Mr. Leader Williams had done excellent work upon inland canals, but unfortunately he had had no experience of tidal estuaries. Mr. Bidderproceeded to re- mind the Committee of certain general principles relative to the Mersey estuary, among which were that the bar flue tuated considerably and was in a critical or " delicat. condition, the tendency being rather to deterioration than otherwise; that the existence of a navigable channel de- pended on the tidal scour, which latter was dependent on the capacity of the tidal reservoir ; and, lastly, that the tidal capacity of the Mersey is preservcd, mainly—he might say solely—by the "fretting" action conseq;uent upon the wandering of the channels from side to side of the broad or upper part of the estuary. None of these conditions was satisfied in the present scheme, which would cause injury to the bar by direct abstraction of tidal capacity, by drawing the flood and the ebb tides tl the Cheshire shore, and by diverting from the upper estuary wator which was new so effective in scouring power. Another result of the proposed works would be fixing of the ebb tide on the Cheshire shore by the removal of the obstacles whicil now prevenh,d, the tide fol- lowing that shore. He argued that the waters of the dyer Weaver exercised a vital influence in maintaining the reyinze of the estuary, and that the proposed works would render it practically impossible for those waters to get into the estuary in. anything like the quantity they now did. In conclusion the learned counsel expressed a hope that the promoters would be sent back once more without their bill.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Mr. Pope began on Tuesday by it reference to his his- tory as a Manchester man, yet urged that the bill was too mighty, andstood in the way of a more modest scheme. The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Companv did not appear, and the London and North-Western Company only appeared in the interests of Garston. He-then spoke of the unprecedented interferences with others, some of them only to be accomplished by unheard of means. He next referred to the Bridgewater and Mersey canals. He argued that the capital would never be raised ; and that eveu the guaranteed capital of,ave million would only yield one million paid up, which would be used in paying for the Bridgewater Canal. He then discussed the probabilities of the canal paying, and argued that the canal proprietors and the Liverpool shipowners would cease competition, and rates be agreed upon. Manchester could only be made a local port. The Committee, as the matter was one of engineering ewe- Hence, should send the prompters back to bring in a Bat confining themselves to what is safe. All that Manchester, needs could be .done without dredging, oven within the limits of deviation. Why should the Committee doctor a phts for them? Ilbe promoters were determined to stick to the scheme of last Year. Their sill should be raised to ad. mit no dredging.—. Mr. Pope spoke two and a half hours.— The Committee adjourned at five o'clock, whilst Mr. Littler was speaking, to Thursday, as Mr. Forster could not attend , on, Wednesday.
