THE FATAL SWING BOAT ACCIDENT. On Monday Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, attended at the White , Hart Hotel, Sankey-aireet, Warrington, to inquire into .the oircumstancesnttend- ing the death of John Lynch (2x), 'a private in the Liverpool Regiment of Militia, stationed at Orford barracks, and son of Edward Lynch, labourer, 13, Carr-lane, West Derby, who on Thursday week fell Out of a swing boat on the fair ground, receiving in- juries from which be died on the following morning at the Infirmary, where he had been removed directly after the accident —Joseph Beckett, 26, Middle Hall Gate, Stockport, son of the proprietor of the swing boats, said that he and another were in charge of them on the Thursday evening in question. The boats were six in number. Deceased and another man in uniform were in one of them, and the second man stood up in the boat, and was several times warned by witness to desist, but took no notice. De- ceased was in the act of standing up when he fell.— A juryman said that on the fair ground there should be a rail to protect from the roundabouts, and another juryman said he thought that it was desirable that it should go forth from that court that the jury deemed it advisable that some proteetion•should be made for the public on the fair ground, both as regarded swing boats and roundabouts. It .was a very dangerous place, especially for young children, for whoni there was no protection. The horses and swing boats were placed so close together that the slightest mistake in a person's footing would cause an accident. A swing boat descending might at any moment knock out a person's brains.—John Jeffries, the companion with whom the deceased was swinging, was then called. He denied that either he or deceased were told to sit down when in the boat. Deceased was standing up from the time when they entered the boat, and both he and witness were sober.—William Hudson, porter at the Infirmary, said that deceased was attended by Drs. Newton and Richmond, and re- ceived every attention.—This completed the evidence, and the coroner, in consequence of their conflicting statements, decided not to allow the expenses of Jef. - fries and Beckett.—The latter witness was called into the room and the coroner said that as soon as the pro- prietor of the boats conducted his business on a safer footing the better it would be for himself. He, and such as he, were making it more and more necessary that the law should be altered, either to prevent these things altogether, or to compel people to conduct them in a safer manner, so that the public, and those who used them, would not be injured. That should be so not only in regard to swingboats, but to round- abouts. If a man would not sit down he (Beckett) should stop the boat. The stoppage of such matters ' was in the hands of the townspeople. There never was a case of that sort, at which the jury did not approve of remarks made by the coroner with regard to these dangerous amusements, and he was sorry that the Warrington people did not either prevent the Corporation letting the ground for such dangerous things, or that the Corporation .id not at least pay a little more regard far the safety of the public. He thought that the attention of the Corporation should be drawn to the matter.—A. verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

A PuBLIC-HOUSE DISTURBANCE. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, James Thompson and John Cheaters were summoned for being disorderly on licensed premiees at Earlestown and refusing to leave when reques- ted on Saturday, the 18th ult.—P.C. Hunt deposed that he and P.C. Lloyd were called to the Prince of Wales Inn by a disturbance, and On going into the vaults they found the two defendants. Thompson was bleeding from the mouth, and using bad language, while the defendant Cheaters had his coat off and using threatening language to Thompson. The landlord, Richard Lythgoe, was requesting them to leave, but they declined to go.—Mr. Richard Lytheoe and P.C. Lloyd gave corroborative evidence, and the defendants were each fined 5s and costs. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

• LONDON, THURSDAY. It IS now certain that the prorogation will take place next week. It might be on Wednesday if the House were in the position in which it usually finds itself at this period of the session. In all ordinary times legislation is so far advanced as to be practi- cally completed before supply, and what has de- tained Parliament in past sessions has been the backwardness of supply. The Financial Secretary to the Treasury's difficulty is the Parnellites' oppor- tunity. When the date ot the prorogation depends upon passing a vote not only on a certain day, but before a certain minute of a day, it is then that Mr. Sexton, Mr. Arthur O'Connor, Mr. Healy, and Mr. Big- gar loom large in the Parliamentary arena. They have nowhere particular to go when the House is up. No quarters open to them are nearly so com- fortable as those provided at Westminster. As far as they are personally concerned they would rather extend the session than not. When it comes to be a question of the desires of other people who want to go yachting, or shooting, or fishing, or travelling, the temptation to thwart them has proved irresist- able. But the Parnellites have been bought with a heavy price, and to do them justice they have, on the whole, fairly kept their bargain. It must have been an enormous temptation to Mr. Biggar yesterday when a quarter to six was ap- proaching and supply not yet finished. If he had risen after the Chancellor of the Exchequer resumed his seat and spoken for only three minutes the mis- chief would have been done. Supply would have been sent over into another day, and the proroga- tion would have been deferred by at least twenty- four hours. What he must have suffered as he sat there with one eye on the clock and the other on the Treasury Bench no one can tell. But he mas- tered the temptation, and just as the three quarters boomed from the clock tower the last vote in Supply was taken. But though it is now in the power of the Govern- ment, as far as Supply is concerned, to prorogue next Wednesday, it is not probable that they will succeed in doing so. They have several bills on ' hand which may take considerable time. The Criminal Law Amendment Bill is of itself sufficient to occupy the undivided attention of the House for a week. In addition there is the bill dealing with the Housing of the Poor, the Irish Land Bill, and one or two others. The hope of a speedy proroga- tion is based upon recollection of the manner in which opposition vanishes under its shadow. Mem- bers have already begun to slip away by scores. Those who remain are hourly tempted to wind up as rapidly as possible and get away. When there are few to listen there are few to talk, and in the absence of the organised obstruction of the Parnell- ites the task of Ministers will be easier than ever.

There is one body of men who are pathetically anxious to bring about the close of the session at the earliest possible moment. These are Her Majesty's Ministers. In the Lords matters have gone with them well enough. They are there in possession of a majority, a condition of affairs which greatly helps to smooth ministerial life: Moreover, Lord Salisbury has refrained from any of that reckless conduct, whether of word or action, that has marked his career in times past. It was notable how on Monday, when the Earl of Milltown was used as an instrument to deal a back-handed blow at the Medical Relief Bill, Lord Salisbury kept entirely free from the squabble. Lord Cran- brook and the Earl of Iddesleigh, were put forward to back up Lord Milltown and thwart Earl Gran- ville. But Lord Salisbury, who was present, took po part in the proceedings. This is all the better i since Sir Michael Beach s fearfully floundering in the Commons. It should, in justice ,to the right hon. baronet, be said that he is not solely to blame for the discredit that has been brought upon the Conservative party since the present Government came into office. The whole of the Cabinet are responsible for the alliance with the Land Leaguers. It is Sir Michael Beach's misfortunethat he is made the mouthpiece of that policy, and is appointed to carry it out. Sir Michael. just before he eame into office, had the misfortune to smirch his personal character by his betrayal of Sir Stafford Northcote. That has deeply prejudiced the House of Commons against him, and made it only too ready to believe the worst. But at best it is a pitiful thing to see a Conserva- tive statesman hand in glove with Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Healy in their denunciation of Earl Spencer and the Irish Executive. Nor was it any better to see Sir Michael Beach on Tuesday joirung Mr. Callan in expression of regret that Mr. Bright, in a moment of honest indignation had in plain language (though not nearly so plain as Lord Randolph Churchill was once accustomed to deliver himself on the same subject) denounced the party of disorder in Ireland. When Parliament is prorogued this apparently in- terminable series of exposures will close, and in the comparative obscurity of Downing-street Ministers will be able quietly to enjoy the sweets of office and the profits of place. It is remarkable with what swiftness and dra- matic completeness the whirlgig of time has brought revenge to Mr. Edmund Yates. Within a year of a trial in which he was implacably pursued by Lord Lonsdale and acrimoniously rebuked by the Lord Chief Justice, he has seen the name of Lord Cole- ridge dragged into a painful scandal, and now Lord Lonsdale is discovered having a rough-and-tumble fight with Sir George Chetwynd in the very centre of fashionable London. Society is, in truth, just now in very bad odour. The outrage in Rotten Row follows close upon the amazing disclosures of profli- gacy in the Aylesford case. Even worse still, be- cause wider in their application, are the stories cur- rent just now in connection with the revelations of the Pall Mall Gazette. Names of some of the most eminent of English public men are bandied about in connection with the revelations, and now the unim- peachable tribune sitting at the Mansion House to investigate the truth of the articles have solemnly declared that the statements made by the Pall Mall Gazette are "substantially true." One of the shadiest features in the case is the positive refusal of the Home Secretary to move in the matter. He has been challenged by the Pall Mall Gazette to prosecute its representatives, and has shaken his head. The Pall Mall plainly says this because he dare not go into the matter. Why he dare not is explained with great freedom in club conversation and dinner table gossip. A.B.C. and D. are said to be personally im- plicated, and the foundations of all that is respecta- ble in society and potent in public life would be shaken if A.B.C. and D. were to be dragged into open court. There is another painful case in which night after night, at all the dinner tables in London society, a world-wide reputation is pulled to pieces. It is ad- mitted that great efforts are being made to keep this case out of court, and everybody is good enough to express the hope that the efforts may prove successful. At the same time names are freely me'ntioned, details are gloated over, and it is made as nearly impossible as may, be to prevent full par- ticulars getting into the papers. I should not be at all surprised to find the affair dealt with at large in some of the cheap weeklies that make Saturday a joy to circles of readers averaging down from the topmost level of half a million. This is Goodwood week, and the weather has en- abled it to justify its title of glorious Goodwood. Apart from its racing interest, Goodwood has a tpeoial significance as being the last milestone of the fashionable season. To be seen in town after • Goodwood week would be almost as discreditable for a person of fashion as if he or she had been fighting in the park or breaking the sanctity of matrimonial relations. Many people who do not mean to go to Goodwood anticipate the end of the season, and already gaps are distinctly visible in the throng in the park, whilst dinner and luncheon engagements,are practically over. The influence of the period now reached tells with great force in the House of Commons. I should say at least a hundred members, regardless of the Appropriation Bill, have left town. Mr. Gladstone has his head quarters at Richmond-terrace, but flits about from country house to country house in the immediate neighbour- hood, and is thoroughly enjoying himself. Like Charles Dickens he has all his life taken a great pleasure in walking about crowded thoroughfares, and now permits himself this luxury unfettered by official cares. He went to see the Mikado last night, a thrilling incident which, as far as I have seen, has escaped the notice of the newspapers, as did his visit to the Inventories the other day. The sale of what was practically two thirds share in the Echo for £lOO,OOO opens the eyes to the value of newspaper property which, as I mentioned the other week, was never so prosperous as now, and with the spread of education is likely to go on pros- pering. A little more than a year ago Mr. Passmore Edwards sold to Messrs. Carnegie and Story two- thirds share of the paper for £70,000, and now has bought it back at an advance of nearly 50 per cent., , which is a pretty good return upon the investment. Of course the purchlise money includes plant and stock which will stand for a considerable item. Moreover, since the sale there has been added to the undertaking a weekly issue which represents a con- siderable amount of added capital.
- - Talking about newspapers, an experienced mana-

ger of a country paper communicated to me the other day a fact which certainly -was surprisimg: It is that amongst the list of novelists 'who have adopted the lucrative and attractive form of pub- lishing their works in the first instance through a syndicate of country weekly papers " Ouida' is a conspicuous failure. So far .frem increasing the sale of a newspaper, her contributions positively re- duce it. The millions who take in their fiction through this medium evidently do not care for im- possibly fascinating Russian Princes, voluptuous sirens, baths of silver, and cloth of gold. The most attractive novelist, according to my authority, is Miss Braddon. In all calculations as to the composition of the new Parliament, it has been taken for granted that Mr. Parnell's following will be at least eighty strong. It may be that this will be so, and it is al- ways well be be prepared for the worst. But there are some considerations in the problem which are not always borne in mind. lam told by an Irish friend that the strength of Mr. Pamell's party in the coming Parliament will very much depend upon the amount of subscriptions which can be extracted during the autumn from the United States, and that the prospect of this being a large one is not so rosy as would-be Parnellite members might wish. Fur- ther, and this is a point which may have much effect, the relations of the Dublin officials of the National League with the provincial lea- ders are by no means as generally cor- dial as the public has .been led to believe. The split which has taken .place over Mr. Edward Har- rington, brother of Mr. Timothy Harrington, M.P., the head centre of the League itself, is an indication of this, and the resignation of Mr. Mathew Harris from membership of the organising committee of the League is equally significant. It is stated that Mr. Harris, who is well remembered for his share in the old Land League troubles, and whose ambition it was to stand for the Ballinasloe Division of Gal- way, has been coolly shunted by Mr. Parnell, partly because he wants to give the seat to a younger man. But another reason is that no fund exists for the payment of members, and this fact, coupled with local feuds, cannot but have its effect at the polls London theatrical managers are complaining that business this summer is even worse than it was last, and they are dismally making up their minds to the fact that the winter on this occasion is not likely to recoup them. The electoral campaign, with its infinitude of meetings, will keep from their doors a vast number of their customary patrons; and however much the political managers upon both sides may plume themselves on the skill with which they have attached so many young men to their respective organisations, their joy is not shared in the managers' rooms of our various theatres.

A BOTANICAL RAMBLE. In carrying out those educational objects which form one of the most admirable features of co-operation in England, the Warrington Co-operative Society during recent years kale in addition to having lectures daring the winter months, promoted each summer one of those " botanical rambles which serve the double purpose of giving its members an opportunity of acquiring knowledge in the pleasantest and meet effective way, and of enjoying a healthful" outing." The, ramble Of this year took place on Saturday afternoon, thP scene of operations being Frodsharn, a place which is excellently adapted for such a purpose alike by the floral wealth of its lanes and fields, its historical and traditional Interest, and its natural scenery. A start was made from Bank Quay station about two o'clock, and a pletsant tide through a thoroughly rural district which at present affords a refreshing variety of newly-mown meadows, of corn already beginning to put on the golden hue of ripeness, and of the dark green leafage of the turnip and potatoe, brought the party to Frodsham. At this time and during the whole of the afternoon the weather was all that could be desired for an outdoor excursion, the heat of the sun being t-mpered by a gentle breeze. The r ntor of the party was the they. J. Freeston, of Staleybridge, a gentlemen excel- lently qualified for an office of this kind both by a fulness of botanical knowledge, and by a not very common facility in imputing tbat knowledge teothers in an easy arta familiar way. On arriving at Frodsham station, a start was at once made in the direction of Overton Hills. A few minutes walk along cite:mimes paths and streets, whose charming irregularity if net pic- turesqueness unmistakeably attest that Frodseam is a town with a lineage, and along past the cburch, which looks what it Is, a venerable remnant of antiquity brought the "botanists" out into a lane which skirts for some distance the base of the bill. Here the business of the day begun, and the party were soon immersed in the mysteries of sepals and petals, of stamens and pistils, of leaves quinate and leaves pinnate, and above all of the bewildering nomenclature of flowers which to the anxieus amateur seems so hopeless a burden for the memory. But attention was not altogether confined to the floral gems of the banks and hedgerows, and various other objects of interest which were come across in the course of the ramble came in for a share of scrutiny and Comment. Such an object, for instance, as one of those huge granite boulders which often puzzle geologists even by their presence amongst rocks of a different order, and ' which lay by the wayside was not passed unnoticed. The why and the wherefore, or tether the wherefrom, of the phenomenon were discussed in the rational and undog- I • matic spirit which becomes modern scientists. The I easy method of the ancients of accounting for all these things by setting them down to the , credit% of one of their many deities or some mythical hero was of course never thought of, and no one , even broached that favourite explanation of a few years When it was customary to ascribe the singular position of the boulders to some occult operation of the flood. In fact. after many more or less probable conjectures it was felt that the mystery was a mystery still, and it was agreed that the stone might be made a peg on which some ingenious and learned local geologist might hang a very interesting dis- course. Another object which came in for a visit by several members of the party was a somewhat spacious cave, the yawning entrance of iv hide could be seen from the road A. diligent exploration, however, did not reveal anything cf note, and certainly nothing was discovered which lay any exweise of sophistry could be twisted into a relic of the pre-historic cave-folk, or even of those pictur- e,que robbers, who, one often reads in story books, used to store their booty and hold high revel in these subterraneen apartments. Nevertheless the absence of anything tangible did not prevent some speculation as to the uses the cavern might have been put to if it then existed, in the days of "stud and strife," when the Saxon WAS slowly but surely dispossessine the Briton of the teorth of Ches- hire, and when Hugh Lupus, the first Earl of Chester, held with the sword his County Palatice against the incur- sions of the "wild Welshmen." The cave having been inspected, the faces of the company were turned towards the refreshment houses on Overton Hills, and after a pleasant saunter, in the course of which some excellent specimens of heath and heather were picked up, these places were reached, and an excellent tea very heartily per. taken of. After tea a short walk along the base of the cliff brought the party to a quiet spot, whence was to be had a fine view of the tows and gardens immediately beneath, and the wind mg course of the Mersey in the distance, and here Mr. Freeston gave an interesting di-course on the plants and flowers which had been collected. In the evening Warriag- ton was again reached about eight o'clock, an afternoon having been pleasantly and instructively spent.

div.head: SATURDAY NIGHT IN CAPE TOWN.
div.p: SATURDAY NIGHT IN CAPE TOWN.
BY A VISITOR.

A few minutes' walk in the calm of a beautiful moonlight evening takes us from our retreat in the picturesque neighbourhood of the Kloof to the busy surroundings of Plein-street, the one place in quiet Cape Town where on a Saturday an Englishman is reminded of the thronged thoroughfares that streets at home present on the evening of that day. How like, and yet how strangely unlike! The din, the noise, the busy shops, a world of buying and selling, and the hubbub, all bring to mind the re- membrance, while the perplexing variety of cos- tume, colour, and speech, multitudinous and ever varying; repels thoughts of home. No, we are but in the street in which once a week the denizens of the metropolis of the Cape meet together in a bustling crowd. The placid waters of the bay are undisturbed, save by the splash of a solitary oar, and the cathedral and suburbs beyond are in sombre and aristocratic quiet. But here in Plein-street, though elsewhere all is deserted, is life and anima- tion abundant. There is much to interest and in- struct and to a stranger something romantic. As we enter there passes a crowd of Delagoa Bay la- bourers, ugly, rough, and uncouth, shouting a Zulu chorus, accompanied with laughter and, to us, strange-sounding language. In peculiar contrast, close by comes a rollicking party from the Austra- lian steamer lying in the bay. They have evidently imbibed sufficient champagne to make them merry, and are passing jests with two ladies—oneof colour and one white—whose blandishments are fascinat- ing. They are as merry as a cruise on shore after a dull .voyage can make them. Declining their jocular invitation to " liquor " at their expense, we move on, attracted by the gestures of a group of young Malays, who chatter in an excited manner at the corner of a street leading to the barracks. They are not attired in their best, but their dress, in its bright contrasting hue, is certainly picturesque, and some of them are not at all bad looking, even to critical European eyes, On the stoep of the Royal some newcomer by the last mail sit superciliously watching, smoking with nonchalance their cheroots. What is this mock scene of life to those who have come from London ! There they sit, interested against their will, while the mass of mingled na- tionality surges on. THE NATIONAL REFORM UNION AT ST.
HELENS.

Sir,—A week or two ago you kindly granted me a lhtle space to comment on the inauguration of a branch of the National Reform Union at St. Helens, and in reply to mf remarks you inserted two communications, signed " Lan- castrian "and "The Secretary." Perhaps you will again oblige me by affording me an opportunity for a few re- marks. The letter of " Lancastrian " is courteous, frank, and manly, but that of" The Secretary" is almost directly the opposite. I thank "Lancastrian "for the information he so kindly gave me, and I regret I cannot do the same to 'the Secretary." The latter correspondent appears tie have jumped to the conclusion that I am " two gettlemen " rolled into one under the signature of " A. Probable Voter," and sneaks of a modern Damon and Pythias, insinuates that lam' two shining lights of Liberalism," and concludes by speaking of my "insane opposition." Surely if this is fit language to a modest inquirer after truth and information, and especially from the secretary of an institution seeking the support of the public, I don't know what is courtesy or friendship. T. disabuse "the secretary of his erroneous impreselons, I may distinctly state that I am not "two gentlemen using one pen," I don't know to whom he refers, lam not acquainted with another person in St. Helens who held the same views that I did, I never consulted another gentleman on the matter, nor en what I should say, and what is more. Important. I alone penned the communication and ' forwarded it to the Examiner without any advice or dicta- tiortfrom anyone. I signed it with a truthful signature, in proof of which I may say that up to the pros nt I never in my life possessed a Parliamentary vote, and consequently never voted, but by the passing of the Franchise Bill I ex- pect to possess that honour and privilege. "The secretary" would appear to me to be the most likely individual to give me the information I sought, but he either seems unable or unwilling to do this. I still maintain that the St. Helens Branch of the National Reform Union is of a "hole and corner" character, and that the proper course for the "promoters" of it to have adopted was to establish it under the auspices or along with the present Liberal organisation in Hardshaw-etreet. They would thereby have been " killing two birds with one stone," for they would not only have secured their own individual members and held their meetings under more promising auspices, but they would have done much to strengthen and re-invigorate the "old horse" which, to my mind, they seem to be throwing over board. It is evident that "the secretary" failed to see the point at which I was driving, owiog to his mental vision having be- come obscured by a bugbear and mythological "Modern Da- mon and Pythias." Perhaps "the secretary " will explain himself a little more clearly for the edification of your readers, and more particularly with the view of enlight- ening, yours, &c,

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
--- Potato blight has appeared extensively in West Cork, and is doing much damage. THE CHESTERFIELDD CUP.—Hermitage, 1; Sandiway, 2; Caltha._3._ Ten ran.
At the Wellingborough Petty Sessions, on Friday, John Wheatley was committed for trial for wife murder.

Mr. Robert Jones, draper, Carnarvon, was drowned on Friday while bathing in Menai Straits. Ibis is the second fatality of a like character in that town this week. An inquest was held at Marylebone, London, on Friday, upon William Coote, bricklayers' labourers, who had died from the bursting of a blood veesel in the brain, owing to the excessive heat of tho weather.

AN IMMENSE SALMON.—The largest salmon ever caught in the Dee was taken on Friday afternoon by Thomas Taylor, fishing at Connal's Quay. The fish is four feet two inches in length ann two feet three inches in girth, and, turns the scale at 50ibs.

Excoarmutnuarox.—The Rev. Coker Adams, rector of Saharn looney, Norfolk, on Friday excommunicated a parishioner aged 82 years, for persistent neglect of the church's ordinances,, and refusal of her ministrations. The excommunication took place before a large congrega- tion.

FUNERAL OF SIR MOSES MONTEFIORE.—The funeral of Sir Moses Monteflore took place at Ramsgate on Friday afternoon. Nearly all the shops were partially closed, and business WAS practically suspended. The weather was dull and cloudy. The funeral rites were of an unassuming character.

THU DISASTER TO Tll,, CHEERFUL.—At Devonport, on Friday morning, Captain Markham and Sub-lieutenant Nicholson were tried by court martial for so negligently navigating H.M.S. Ilecia that she sunk the steamship Cheerful, on the night of the 2(hti inst. Evidence was given of a fog prevailing, and the orders of the accused to give all ships a wide berth. Evidence was also given that the Hecla steers uncertainly, and her rudder is too small. Loan RANDOLPH CHURCHILL —The Standard (Causer-. %%vivo) says :—The truth is, that Lord Randolph Churchill is a mach over-rated man. He is now verging upon middle age, and has reached a time of life when even flighty minds ought to sober down. But that is what he cannot do. His almost incredible ignorance of affairs, his boyish delight in offering the crudest insults to men who have been fifty years in the service of the State, his pranks, his blunders, are ceasing to amuse. Those entrusred with the formation of the Conservative Government did not see their way to dis- regard him. It was a game of "brag," and their allowed themselves to be beaten. They have, however, paid dearly for their prize. •

div.head: THREE PERSONS DROWNED.
div.p: THREE PERSONS DROWNED.

A shocking fatality mirkzd the close of Bray Regal ta on Thursday night. Six persons, of whom five were women, went afloat in a punt, and, after proceeding some way, the craft capsized, throwing its occupants in the wa.er. A man named Hale managed to escip*„ and also two servants; but a Mrs. Ford and two sister& were drowned. RAILWAY COLLISION.—FIVX PERSONS KILLED.

The Central News Shepton Mallet correspondent tele- arapbs :—A'disastrous railwiy accident occurred on the Somerset and Dorset Joint Line on Friday, between Shepten Mallet and Chilcompton. The fast train had just left Shep- ton Mallet when it caught up and ran into a goods train ahead, at a pace called Binnegar. Five passengers were killed and several injured. The line where the accident occurred is at present a single one, but the company are now employed in laying down an addiaional set of metals.

div.p: _THE CHOLERA IN SPAIN.
A Central News telegram, dated Madrid, Friday morning, says :—The cholera returns- issued this morning show that daring the past twenty-four hours there have been 2,616 fresh cases and 1,039 deaths.

div.head: FUNERAL OF GENERAL GRANT.
div.p: FUNERAL OF GENERAL GRANT.

NEW YORK, FEIDAY.—Mrs. Grant has asked President Cleveland the names of those whom he appointed to act as pall-bearers at her late husband's funeral, requesting him if he has nominated any prominent army officers, to ap- point also one who took a prominent part in the war of secession. President Cleveland has informed Mrs. Grant that her wish will be carried out.

div.head: LAST NIGHTS PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHTS PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

MISCELLANEOUS.—The House met a quarter to one o'clock, when Prince Henry of Batrenberg presented himself at the Bar and took the oath of allegiance preparatory to naturalisation. The sitting was then suspended till four o'clock, when the royal assent was given to 38 Acts of Par- liament, including Exchequer and Treasury Bills, Public Health (Ships' cite.) Acts. Prince Henry of Battenberg's Naturalisation Bill was read a third time and peso]. The Earldom of Mar Reatitation Bill also passed.—The Earl of WHITYSS drew attention to what be termed the Socialiat tendency in the effects of legislation of the last 15 years:— The subject then dropped after some remarks from Lord Salisbury and Earl Granville.—The Medical Relief Dis- qualification Removal Bill, Parliamentary Elections Cor- • rupt Practices Bill. and Patent Law Amendment till pas- sed the second reading. The House adjourned at half-past six. HOUSES OF COMMONS.

The House met at four o'clock. PRINCE HENRY.—On tbe motion for the second reading of Prince Battenborg Naturalisation Bill, Sir W. LAWSON asked what the bill was for, and why it was being hurried through.—The CHANCELLOR of the Itxcwaquwa said the bill was to naturalise Prince Henry of Battenberg.—Mr. BROADHURST thought it extraordinary to pass a bill not printed, and relative to a gentleman they knew nothing about. (No, no, and laughter.)—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said iu fact the bill ought to have been passed before the marriage. (ILoud laughtcr.)—The bill was read a second time and passed through its other stages. ` THE PROTECTION. 0.7 YOUNG GIRLS.—The House went into committee on the Criminal Law Amendments Bill.— On the consideration of clause three, which provided punishment for procuring the defilement of women by threats and fraud, Ma: HOPWOOD proposed to omit the first subsection to the clause which made it a misdemeanor punishable with two years' imprisonment.—Sfr W. Hsu- cocrwr objected to Mr. Hit:mood's amendment, which even- tually was withdrawn—Sir R. Coss moved a • subsection bringing those under the clause who administ.red, applied, or caused to be taken by any woman or girl any stupifying or overpowering drug with intent to commit an offence.— Mr. M'Coax wished the amendment so worded as to punish the men who committed the offence as well as the person who administered the drug.—Mr. STANSFIELD wished for the introduction of words to provide for the administration of intoxicating liquors to excess —The ATTORNEY-GENERAL expressed Ma wilßngness to add to the amendment words so as to stupify or overpower.—The amendment as to that addition was accepted, and the clause agreed to.—Clause 4, which provided special punishment for offences on girls under twelve years of age, was next proposed.—Captain PRICE moved to omit the word twelve and insert thirteen.— Sir R. Cnoss said he would adopt thirteen, but he strongly objected to increase the age beyond that.—Mr. S. MORLEY wished the age should be fourteen —On the question that thirteen be inserted the Committee divided—Ayes, 76; noes, 58.—Mr. H. FOWLER moved the addition of words to the clause by which the court before whom such person was 1 convicted should have the power to direct that such person 1 might be whipped.—after a lengthy discussion the Com- mittee divided. For the amendment, 91; against, 125. Mr. ACEERS moved an amendment to provide that it should be a sufficient defenca to any charge brought under the clause for persons so charged to state their belief that the girl was above the age of thirteen.

SUICIDE OF A FAD,ltin AT PADGATE.—Yesterday afternoon an inquest Was: held in the " Padgate Stocks" Inn, Padgate, relative to the death of a farmer named John Gilbert, who committed suicide ; by hanging on Tuesday afternoon. The coroner was Mr. Brighouse. Ann Gilbert, daughter of the de- I ceased, said her father was 60 years of age. She last saw him alive about half-past three on Tuesday , afternoon. He had been very poorly lately, and had I been attended by Dr. Joseph, of Warrington. He had given up his farm a few months ago, when there was a sale, and he had been rather low spirited I since then.—John Gilbert, son of the deceased, said f he found his father suspended from a beam in the I barn on Tuesday evening last, between seven and ; eight o'clock. He immediately went to seek a ; young man named Thomas Unsworth, who cut the body down.—Thomas Unsworth stated that on be- I ing called by last witness to the barn he saw de- ceased hanging by the neck to a beam which was ; about ten feet from the floor. There was a short ' ladder standing against the wall, from which de- ceased had apparently swung himself, lie was dead, and seemed to have been dead two or three hours. Deceased had appeared depressed for some time, ever since he had to leave his farm. When he (witness) was called he suspected that deceased had committed suicide.—A verdict to the effect that , deceased committed suicide whilst in a state Of tem-, porary insanity was returued,
WARRINGTON. BA ins HOLlDA.y.—Several excursions are arranged by the London and North-Western Railway and Cheshire Lines. Details are given in another column,

DARESBURY Beiloor,.—We understand that Mr. Logan, of Dareabury 'Hall, has been nominated governor of the Daresbury School in place of Mr. Chadwick who has resigned. BAND or HOPE GALA.—On Monday a grand procession and gala will be held in connection with the Warrington Band of Hope Union. The procession will leave the Town Hall at 1-30 o'clock, and the ;gala will be field in the field adjoiaing St. James's Church. WORKMEN'S TRIP.-013 Saturday the. workrople of Messrs. John H. Fleming and Co., of Fennel-street Tannery, together with their wives and children, had a trip to Blackpool. A gratuity was given to each towards the payment of expenses.. The weather was fine, and the outing a pleasant one. DEATH PROM SUNSTROKR.—An inquest was held at Culcheth, near Wallington, on Tuesday, .respect- lag the death of a boy named. Robert Batteraby, who, was found ill in a field, and. soon afterwards died.. The evidence showed that death was caused by sunstroke, and a verdict to that effect was returned. ST. BARNADAS' CHOHL—On'atturday the mem- bers of the choir of St. BarnabaW Church, at the invi- tation of the Vicar, the Rev.. G. Allton, huff an excursion to Blackpool, when at pleasant dabs was spell:, The party were invited' by the vicar, to, dinner and tea. Warrington was reached again at. about ten o'clock in the evening. OccesioNAL Counr.—At an Occasional Court held on Monday, before Messrs. J. Tinsley and P. Stubs, four men named Asher Wood, Patrick Kelly, Bernard' Mannion, and Patrick Burns, were charged with, ganabliUg by playing cards in Arpley Fields, on the 26th July. Wood and Kelly were each fined 10 and costs, and the others were dismissed. Sr. JAMES'S CHURCH Cirorn.—On Monday the younger members of this choir had their annual trip to Blackpool, and greatly enjoyed themselves. The weather was fine, and the sea, it being high tide in the mo-ning was rather boisterous. The party took tea together in the afternoon, and the retarn journey was commenced at 6-45, Warrington being reached at about nine o'clock. TEA PARTY AND BALL AT BURTONWOOD.—The annual summer tea party and dance took place in the Burtonwood Church Schools, on Thursday even- ing. The room had been very nicely decorated. About sixty persons sat down to a most substantial tea. Afterwards the room was cleared for dancing, which was spiritedly indulged in to the strains of Messrs. Appleton's (Earlestown) string band. COCKHEDGE MILLS EXCURSION.—The annual ex- cursion in connection with Cockhedge Mills took place on Satuxday, when about 1,000 of: the em- ployes went to Blackpool. The excursion train left Bank Quay Station a few minutes after six in the morning, and arrived at Warrington again 'at about ten o'clock in the evening. Extension tickets were allowed those who desired to remain at Blackpool until Monday. The weather was fine and the trip an enjoyable. one. THE STIPPOSED ATTEMPTED BURGLA.RY.—At the Borough Court, yesterday, Thomas Burke; a. soldier, stationed at Aigly-street Barracks, was brought up on remand charged with being found on the premises of William Mather, 95, Buttermarket- street, on the 24th of July, with intent to commit a felony. The circumstances of the case; which have previously been made public, are, briefly, that pri- soner was seen by a inan who gave information to the police to. enter the house in question by the window in the middle of the night. On endeavour- ing to leave.by the same way 'he was promptly.ar- rested. He now admitted going into the house, but saidthat he.was under the influence of drink,. and did not know what he was doing.—He was sent to prison for • fourteen days. SUDDEN DEATH.—Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the White Hart Intel, Sankey-street, on Monday afternoon, respecting the death of a man named William Posthen, of Great Bridge, Horsley Heath, Tipton, Staffordshire,. 38 years of age, an ironworker, who was found lying unconscious in a field opposite Woolston Hall, under circumstances previously made public. He was re- moved to the Workhouse at Warrington, where •he died in about an hour's time without having re- gained consciousness. An inquest was subsequently held, and adjourned for a post-mortem examina- tion of the body to be made, and efforts directed to lead to identification. Dr. Spinks, medical Officer at the Workhouse, now reported the result of the ex- amination, and expressed the opinion that deceased died from.apoplexy. Evidence of identification having been grven, the jury returned a verdict iii. accordance with the medical evidence.

Dr. Grace was, for the thirty tiane during the week, out I.b.w. In a match between two counties not much known to cricketing fame, Cutnberland and Northumberland, Mr. C. Tobin, a light blue of last year, has just accomplished a wonderful performance with the hat. He secured 52 out of a total of 145, and dismissed no fewer than 16 of his oppo- nents for 49 runs-8 for 29 in the first innings, and 8 for 20 in the second innings. It has been arranged that a team of English amateur cricketers will visit America. They will leave Liverpool on the 20th pros.
